Appendix.title: A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration
Appendix.source: Concepts/A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration.md
Appendix.Content: A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

For a fixed-point iteration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>G</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> </math> is a contraction with Lipschitz constant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo><</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> on a region containing the iterates and its fixed point. Then the remaining error is bounded by the next step divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math>: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>≤</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The assumption is essential; a small step alone does not prove convergence because stagnation or a failed update can also make changes tiny. In implementation, report the contraction evidence or a suitable residual bound and keep failure distinct from success. This turns an observed update into a conditional, checkable estimate rather than a guess. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math> and the latest step is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>6</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, this bound is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mo>×</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>6</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, conditional on the contraction proof.

Appendix.title: Algorithmic stability
Appendix.Content: Algorithmic stability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A numerical problem can be sensitive even when an algorithm handles it well. Stability describes whether the finite-precision algorithm introduces only the error expected from rounding, often by showing that its output exactly solves a nearby problem. Backward stability is one useful form; forward stability asks directly how close the computed answer is to the exact answer for the original input. The claim must name its assumptions, arithmetic model, and problem class. For example, a stable linear solver can still have a large forward error on an ill-conditioned matrix. Stability therefore belongs beside conditioning, not in its place. A dot product with a small residual can still conceal an ill-conditioned problem, so report which notion of stability is actually supported.

Appendix.title: Axial depth and Euclidean range
Appendix.Content: Axial depth and Euclidean range
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Axial depth measures distance along the camera’s forward axis; Euclidean range measures distance from the camera centre along the viewing ray. With a right-handed view frame looking along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>Z</mi> </math>, positive axial depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>z</mi> </math>, while range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>z</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </msqrt> </math>. They agree only on the optical axis. For a unit ray direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> <mo><</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, a range measurement converts to axial depth as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>r</mi> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msub> </math>. A range sensor and a perspective depth buffer may therefore encode different quantities. Applying a depth-buffer formula directly to a range image distorts reconstructed geometry away from the image centre. At view point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, axial depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>12</mn> </math> while range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>13</mn> </math>, a visible distinction off-axis.

Appendix.title: Bandit exploration and regret
Appendix.Content: Bandit exploration and regret

A multi-armed bandit models sequential choices when only the reward of the chosen action is observed. It separates exploitation—choosing what currently looks best—from exploration—choosing an uncertain action to learn about it.

Let arm <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math> have unknown mean reward <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>μ</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </math>. Over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>T</mi> </math> rounds, one common stationary pseudo-regret benchmark is

where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>μ</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> </math> is the largest fixed-arm mean and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> is the chosen arm at round <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math>.
Regret is meaningful only relative to the benchmark and environment assumptions. In a nonstationary problem, “best fixed arm” may be the wrong target.
UCB intuition
Upper-confidence-bound methods choose an action using an optimistic estimate such as

where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> </math> is the number of samples from arm <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math>. The uncertainty bonus shrinks with evidence and is larger for rarely tried arms.

The derivation of a confidence radius depends on reward bounds/noise assumptions. Reusing a textbook radius for arbitrary unbounded timing noise or correlated frame measurements removes the theorem that motivated it.
Nonstationary workloads

Render cost, network latency, cache behavior and user demand can change. An all-history mean adapts slowly after a regime shift. Sliding-window estimates, exponential discounting or explicit change detection trade statistical efficiency in stationary periods for responsiveness.
Adaptive sampling can change an estimator

Choosing what to measure next based on observed rewards is useful for experimental efficiency, but it can make a naive final average biased toward frequently selected outcomes. Adaptive experiment allocation and unbiased Monte Carlo integration are different problems.
When selection probabilities are known, importance weighting can correct some adaptive sampling schemes:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>T</mi> </mfrac> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>t</mi> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Very small selection probabilities can make the variance enormous, so mathematical unbiasedness does not guarantee a practical estimator.
Graphics/research use

Bandits are plausible for choosing which configuration to benchmark, which reconstruction region deserves another expensive measurement, or which experiment to run next. They should not be inserted into a pixel estimator on the assumption that maximizing a reward signal automatically preserves the target rendering integral.

The direct mathematics expansion is at Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Choose the next measurement using the geometry of what is still unknown. The graphics narrative connects adaptive computation at Continuous Notes/University - Worlds, Images and Inference - Graphics, Vision and Photography#From Random Samples to Deliberate Computation.
Related: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence, Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling, Sampling support and missing strata.

Appendix.title: Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
Appendix.Content: Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Barycentric weights reconstruct a triangle point as an affine combination. The weights sum to one; nonnegative weights describe points inside or on a nondegenerate triangle. Dot-system solves on off-plane inputs describe their projection, not proven surface membership.

The panel sensor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>12</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and corner temperatures <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>20</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>40</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>50</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> interpolate to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>35</mn> </math>.

Extend the existing interpolation note with the geometric meanings that make triangle rasterization and camera calibration easier to reason about. For triangle vertices <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>, a point inside can be written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>, where the weights sum to one and are nonnegative. Each weight is the area of the opposite subtriangle divided by the full triangle area; equivalently it is a signed edge-distance normalized by altitude. The weights therefore provide both a point-in-triangle test and attribute interpolation. They also reveal a limitation: screen-space weights do not linearly interpolate a 3D attribute after perspective projection. Interpolate reciprocal depth and attribute divided by depth, then divide the interpolated values to recover perspective-correct texture coordinates or colors.

Appendix.title: Bracketed and open root solvers
Appendix.Content: Bracketed and open root solvers
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A root solver seeks <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. A bracketed method maintains an interval whose endpoints have opposite signs; continuity then guarantees at least one root remains inside, and bisection provides a predictable shrinking error bound. Open methods such as secant and Newton can converge faster near a well-behaved simple root, but they may diverge, encounter a zero derivative, or leave the relevant domain. A safeguarded hybrid uses a bracket for global protection and accepts fast proposals only when they preserve progress. Residual size alone does not certify root accuracy when the root is poorly conditioned, and discontinuous functions do not satisfy the sign-change guarantee.

Appendix.title: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation
Appendix.source: Concepts/Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation.md
Appendix.Content: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A Bézier curve blends control points with Bernstein basis weights. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, so the curve remains in the control points’ convex hull and reaches its first and last control points at the endpoints. De Casteljau’s repeated linear interpolation evaluates the curve using numerically straightforward convex combinations; the intermediate levels also reveal subdivision geometry. A cubic Bézier’s endpoint tangents depend on its first and last control-polygon edges, so moving a handle changes direction and scale. The convex-hull guarantee applies to the curve parameter interval; extrapolation outside it loses that containment property. Subdivide the curve before tessellation when screen-space curvature changes rapidly; parameter steps alone do not guarantee uniform pixel error.

Appendix.title: Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Appendix.Content: Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

A gauge freedom is a coordinated change to unknown scene and camera parameters that leaves every measured image unchanged. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, translating and rotating the entire reconstruction changes only the chosen world frame, while a common scale change of points and camera translations preserves projections; absolute metric scale therefore needs an external reference. Observability asks which local parameter changes produce distinguishable measurements. Linearizing reprojection residuals gives a Jacobian; its weighted information tensor or matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>J</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>W</mi> <mi>J</mi> </math> reveals weak parameter combinations through small eigenvalues after gauge directions are fixed. Example: adding more points to one planar, nearly fronto-parallel view may reduce pixel noise while focal length and distance remain strongly coupled. These conclusions assume a stated camera/scene model, correctly associated observations, and local linearization; the information matrix diagnoses local constraints, not global uniqueness. Report uncertainty only after fixing the gauge and specifying the observation noise model.

Example: A monocular map can be uniformly enlarged with all camera translations enlarged by the same factor and render the same images; a known baseline or measured object length fixes that scale gauge.

Assumptions: The gauge statement assumes calibrated monocular perspective cameras and no metric prior.; The information-matrix interpretation is local and depends on residual weighting and parameterization.

Appendix.title: Common probability distributions and their assumptions
Appendix.source: Concepts/Common probability distributions and their assumptions.md
Appendix.Content: Common probability distributions and their assumptions
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Distribution families encode different experiment structures. Bernoulli models one binary trial; binomial counts independent trials with the same success probability; uniform assigns constant density or mass over a specified support; Gaussian models a bell-shaped law through mean and covariance; exponential describes memoryless waiting under a constant event rate; Poisson counts events in a fixed exposure under independent, stationary event assumptions. Their formulas are not interchangeable labels: each relies on support and sampling assumptions. Moments summarize center and spread but may fail to exist for heavy-tailed laws. Multivariate Gaussian models also require a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance, with positive definiteness needed for an ordinary full-dimensional density. Identify the experiment, parameter meanings, and dependence structure before selecting a distribution. The same family can model measurement noise, a prior, or a sampling proposal, which are different roles.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Complex numbers and planar rotations
Appendix.Content: Complex numbers and planar rotations
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

Complex multiplication combines planar rotation and scaling. A unit complex multiplier represents a rotation; its conjugate gives the inverse. A two-component storage tuple is not automatically a rotation.

Multiplication by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> sends <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Zero collapses the plane rather than representing any rotation.

Appendix.title: Conditional Gaussians and Schur complements
Appendix.Content: Conditional Gaussians and Schur complements
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Conditioning one block of a jointly Gaussian vector on another produces a Gaussian conditional law under the usual nonsingular assumptions. Its mean shifts by the cross-covariance times the inverse observed-block covariance, while its covariance is the Schur complement Σbb−ΣbaΣaa⁻¹Σab. That conditional covariance is positive semidefinite: insert the vector (−Σaa⁻¹Σabv,v) into the joint covariance quadratic form. If the joint covariance is positive definite, the Schur complement is positive definite. The conditional covariance does not depend on the observed value, although the conditional mean does. This formula links Bayesian updating, Gaussian elimination, and block linear systems. Singular observed blocks require a compatible degenerate-Gaussian treatment or a rank-revealing method; blindly applying an inverse is invalid.

Appendix.title: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
Appendix.Content: Confidence intervals and sequential evidence
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A confidence interval is a procedure with repeated-sample coverage under stated assumptions; it is not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter. A normal interval for a mean uses a known population standard deviation or an approximation justified by the central limit theorem. With unknown scale and IID normal observations, the Student t distribution accounts for estimating the standard deviation. Heavy tails, sample dependence, multiple comparisons, and optional stopping can invalidate simple textbook guarantees. Adaptive algorithms that stop when a fixed-sample interval looks narrow need sequentially valid methods or a separately justified stopping rule. Report the target, sampling unit, dependence structure, estimator bias, interval procedure, stopping policy, and independent-run count. A narrow interval around a biased estimator measures precision about its expectation, not correctness of the target.

Appendix.title: Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation
Appendix.Content: Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

If an approximation has leading error <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, halving the step reduces that term by about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </math>. Comparing results at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> </math> estimates the observed order; Richardson extrapolation combines two resolutions to cancel the leading term when the assumed order is valid. The method is diagnostic, not magic: measurements must be in the asymptotic regime, the same mathematical quantity must be computed at each resolution, and roundoff or stochastic noise must not dominate. For Euler integration, first-order refinement predicts the leading error to halve. Record the sequence and residuals rather than reporting an order from one pair alone. Ratios near an expected power provide evidence, but one noisy ratio is not a convergence study.

Appendix.title: Convex combinations and convex hulls
Appendix.Content: Convex combinations and convex hulls
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

Affine point combinations have weights summing to one. Convex combinations additionally have nonnegative weights. A convex set contains every segment between its members; a convex hull is the smallest such set containing supplied points.
The panel is the convex hull of its corners. A filled disk is convex; its boundary alone is not.

Appendix.source: Concepts/Coordinate frames and change of basis.md
Appendix.Content: Coordinate frames and change of basis
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

A frame gives an origin and independent axes relative to another frame. Its matrix maps local coordinates to that parent description. Changing description uses the inverse destination frame followed by the source frame; active motion and passive coordinate change answer different questions.
Reconstruction cue: Coordinates from frame A to frame B use inverse(F_B) times F_A.

Appendix.Content: Coordinate handedness and orientation

Definition and mechanism

Handedness is the sign of an ordered basis relative to a chosen orientation. A reflection reverses it; a proper rotation preserves it. It does not specify up axis, camera direction or matrix storage order.

Swapping two axes flips the sign.

Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

Appendix.title: Cubic Hermite interpolation
Appendix.Content: Cubic Hermite interpolation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A cubic Hermite segment is determined by endpoint values and endpoint tangent data. With normalized <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, its four basis polynomials blend the two endpoint positions and two tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to the parameter, so physical-time derivatives must be scaled by segment duration: a velocity in units per second is not interchangeable with a tangent per normalized parameter. Hermite curves are useful when a camera path or animation must pass through known positions while exposing direct control over its entry and exit directions. The endpoint constraints determine one cubic polynomial; continuity between adjacent segments still requires compatible endpoint tangents.

Appendix.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
Appendix.source: Concepts/Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem.md
Appendix.Content: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A definite integral accumulates a quantity over an interval, with sign and units determined by the integrand and integration variable. Riemann sums approximate this accumulation by weighted samples; under suitable regularity conditions their limit defines the integral. The fundamental theorem connects accumulation and differentiation: an antiderivative evaluates the net integral, and the derivative of an accumulated integral recovers its integrand when continuity conditions hold. This link explains why integrating velocity gives displacement and why a variable upper-limit integral solves a simple differential equation. Definite integral, indefinite antiderivative, and geometric area are related but not interchangeable ideas. The integration variable is a dummy variable, so name it distinctly from the endpoint. Integrals also form the target of Monte Carlo estimators, where measure and sampling density must match.

Appendix.title: Derivative as a local linear map
Appendix.source: Concepts/Derivative as a local linear map.md
Appendix.Content: Derivative as a local linear map
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be.

Appendix.title: Differentiation rules and chain rule
Appendix.Content: Differentiation rules and chain rule
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Differentiation rules let us build derivatives from simpler functions. Linearity handles sums and constant factors; the product and quotient rules account for both factors changing; the chain rule handles nested mappings. For a composition, the derivative of the outer function is evaluated at the inner output and multiplied by the derivative of the inner function. In multiple dimensions, this becomes matrix multiplication of Jacobians in composition order. Elementary rules for powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, and inverse trigonometric functions follow from limits and implicit relations. These rules are the local sensitivity algebra used by automatic differentiation and gradient-based fitting. Each rule has a domain: quotient denominators must be nonzero, logarithms require positive arguments, and inverse trigonometric derivatives can become singular at boundary values.

Appendix.title: Directional and total derivatives
Appendix.Content: Directional and total derivatives
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A directional derivative measures first-order change along a chosen direction. For a differentiable scalar field, it is the gradient paired with that direction; for a vector map, the Jacobian acts on the direction. The total derivative accounts for every input coordinate changing according to a path, combining partial derivatives with the rates of the coordinates themselves. A direction need not be normalized: normalization changes whether the derivative is per unit distance or per unit parameter. This distinction matters in signed-distance queries, motion paths, and parameterized camera projections. The total derivative clarifies the chain rule: if a state depends on time and an output depends on that state, the time rate is the local derivative composed with the state velocity. These are local statements, not global linearity claims.

Appendix.title: Discretization, truncation, and roundoff
Appendix.Content: Discretization, truncation, and roundoff
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Discretization replaces a continuous object or domain with a finite grid; truncation omits terms or limits an iterative expansion; roundoff comes from finite-precision arithmetic. They have different causes and respond to different changes. Refining a spatial grid may reduce discretization error while increasing computation. Adding more terms can reduce truncation error. Increasing precision or reformulating arithmetic can reduce roundoff, though a poor algorithm may still dominate. A signed-distance field sampled too coarsely can lose a thin feature entirely, while an ODE’s Euler step has a local truncation error even under exact arithmetic. An error budget should distinguish these mechanisms instead of calling every disagreement “numerical error.”

Appendix.title: Dot products and orthogonality
Appendix.Content: Dot products and orthogonality
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

An inner product provides a scalar measurement of two vectors. In orthonormal real coordinates the dot is a sum of component products. Its geometric form is length product times angle cosine. Orthogonality means zero inner product; zero itself has no angle.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>⋅</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>6</mn> </math>, while the cosine is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>6</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo>⋅</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> </math>. Coordinate dotting assumes the correct metric.

Appendix.title: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces

An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a square linear map scales by its eigenvalue. The eigenspace is the null space of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>I</mi> </math>. Real symmetric matrices have an orthonormal eigenbasis; general matrices may be defective or have sensitive eigenvectors.

Appendix.title: Expectation, covariance, and dependence
Appendix.Content: Expectation, covariance, and dependence
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity, and variance is the expected squared deviation from that average. Covariance measures how two centered quantities vary together; correlation scales it to a unitless linear-association measure. For a random vector, the covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because every directional quadratic form equals a variance. Zero covariance does not usually imply independence, except under special joint Gaussian conditions. Conditional expectation and total-variance identities decompose uncertainty into within-group spread and variation between group means. These moments drive Monte Carlo error analysis, Gaussian geometry, and linear uncertainty propagation. An empirical covariance depends on sample convention and denominator; Bessel correction concerns unbiased population-variance estimation under IID sampling, not a universal change to descriptive covariance.

Appendix.title: Exterior products and geometric algebra
Appendix.Content: Exterior products and geometric algebra
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

Exterior products represent oriented higher-dimensional elements without forcing them into vectors. A wedge is antisymmetric and bilinear; a bivector has grade two. Euclidean geometric algebra combines inner and exterior products into one product. Higher-dimensional sums of bivectors need not be a single plane.

The plane element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>I</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi> </mrow> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> satisfies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>I</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, connecting plane rotations to complex-number behavior.

Appendix.title: Finite differences and step-size balance
Appendix.Content: Finite differences and step-size balance
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Finite differences estimate derivatives from sampled function values. Forward and backward differences use one-sided samples and have first-order truncation error; central differences use samples on both sides and usually have second-order truncation error for smooth functions. Making the step arbitrarily small is not always better: subtractive cancellation and evaluation noise grow as the step shrinks, while truncation error grows when it is too large. The useful step balances these effects and depends on scale, precision, and function noise. Finite differences are valuable for black-box sensitivities and gradient checks, but they are not automatic differentiation and can fail near discontinuities or branch changes. A numerical gradient check should compare directional derivatives, use scale-aware steps, and avoid interpreting one tolerance pass as proof that every derivative path is correct.

Appendix.title: Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
Appendix.source: Concepts/Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images.md
Appendix.Content: Function contracts: domains, codomains, and images
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. Its domain states which inputs are valid; its codomain states the declared output set; its image is the subset actually reached. These sets affect whether an inverse exists and whether a formula is defined at a boundary. For example, squaring maps the real line into nonnegative outputs but is not one-to-one until its domain is restricted to nonnegative values. In a camera map, division by depth makes zero depth invalid, while a positive-forward convention further restricts visible points. Treating these as contracts makes composition safer: the output of one function must lie in the next function’s domain. A typed implementation can encode some, but not all, of these mathematical restrictions.

Appendix.title: Gram matrices and coordinate metrics
Appendix.Content: Gram matrices and coordinate metrics
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

A Gram matrix stores pairwise basis inner products. Coordinate vectors measure physical dot products through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>G</mi> <mi>d</mi> </math>. It is positive semidefinite, and positive definite for independent generators. It records metric geometry but not orientation.

The basis <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mtable columnspacing="1em" rowspacing="4pt"> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> </math>. Coordinates <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> give squared length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>13</mn> </math>, not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>5</mn> </math>.

Appendix.Content: Hardware depth-buffer linearization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Perspective projection maps axial distance nonlinearly into NDC depth. For a declared projection depth row <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </math>, solve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; finite conventional, finite reversed, infinite reversed, and OpenGL-style conventions have different coefficients or NDC conversions. The depth sample must first be interpreted in the same range and direction used by the projection matrix. This is why a single generic formula without an API and projection contract is unsafe. Verify near and far endpoints, test round trips over a range of distances, and handle an infinite-far endpoint such as reversed depth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> explicitly. Near/far endpoint checks catch sign mistakes immediately; interior round trips then test scaling and finite precision.

Appendix.title: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
Appendix.Content: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints.

An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length.

University course development

Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Dividing the first three components by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>.
Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration
Phase 11 camera development

Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.

Appendix.title: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities
Appendix.Content: Implicit differentiation and parameter sensitivities
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Implicit differentiation obtains how a solution changes when it is defined by an equation rather than an explicit formula. If a state satisfies F(y,θ)=0 and the Jacobian with respect to y is invertible, differentiating gives dy/dθ=−(∂F/∂y)⁻¹(∂F/∂θ). This can differentiate equilibrium states, constrained optima, and roots without unrolling every solver iteration. For a converged optimizer, differentiating stationarity and constraint conditions yields sensitivity equations, but active-set changes, nonunique solutions, singular Jacobians, and imperfect convergence complicate the result. Continuous sensitivity equations propagate derivatives alongside an ODE; adjoint methods can reduce cost when there are many parameters and few scalar outputs. These are modeling tools with assumptions, not a guarantee that every algorithmic branch is differentiable.

Appendix.title: Interpolation versus approximation
Appendix.Content: Interpolation versus approximation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Interpolation reproduces every prescribed sample exactly, while approximation minimizes or controls an error criterion and may miss the observations. The distinction matters when data are noisy: a high-degree interpolant can fit measurement noise and oscillate between samples, while a lower-complexity approximation can better represent the underlying trend. In texture reconstruction, the samples themselves often define the represented signal, so interpolation is an appropriate reconstruction rule. In calibration, observations have uncertainty, so fitting a model may be more defensible. Neither method is automatically superior; choose based on the meaning of the data, the error measure, and whether evaluation stays within or extrapolates beyond the sampled domain.

Appendix.title: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling
Appendix.Content: Inverse, rejection, and importance sampling
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Sampling transforms convert simpler random inputs into a target law. Inverse-CDF sampling maps a uniform value through a quantile function; rejection sampling accepts proposal draws according to a bounded target-to-proposal ratio; importance sampling estimates an integral by dividing each sampled integrand by the actual proposal density. Each method requires correct support and endpoint handling. Importance sampling is unbiased when the proposal covers every contributing region and the weighted contribution is integrable; finite variance additionally requires the integral of f²/p to be finite. Rejection sampling needs a valid finite envelope. Discrete floating-point inputs can hit boundaries that have zero probability in an ideal continuous model. Report the density with its measure and use the same measure in the estimator. A proposal that misses target support cannot be repaired by a larger weight.

Appendix.title: LU factorization and reusable solves
Appendix.Content: LU factorization and reusable solves

LU stores elimination as triangular factors. With row pivoting in this vault’s convention, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mi>U</mi> </math>; apply the same permutation to each right-hand side, then solve one lower- and one upper-triangular system. Factorization cost is amortized across repeated solves.
Use it when: solving square general systems, especially with multiple right-hand sides.

Developed in Phase 8: The multipliers used to eliminate entries become the lower factor, while the remaining upper triangle records the reduced system; with row exchanges the convention is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mi>U</mi> </math>. The runnable pivoted LU reference traces permutation, factor storage, status, and repeated forward/back substitution on actual values. runnable pivoted LU lab · forward and backward solves

Appendix.title: Latin-hypercube sampling
Appendix.Content: Latin-hypercube sampling
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Latin-hypercube sampling divides each coordinate axis into <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math> equal strata and uses a permutation so every sample occupies one stratum per dimension. With randomized within-stratum positions and randomized permutations, each sample has uniform marginal coordinates; samples are dependent by design. This can improve coverage for some integrands at arbitrary sample counts, including counts that do not form a square grid. It does not guarantee lower variance for every function, and IID variance formulas cannot be applied without accounting for dependence. Test exact stratum coverage deterministically, then compare estimator error over repeated randomized trials for the intended integrand. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>5</mn> </math>, each axis still receives five strata, avoiding the missing-cell bias of taking five cells from a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> <mo>×</mo> <mn>3</mn> </math> grid.

Appendix.title: Limits and continuity
Appendix.Content: Limits and continuity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point, even when the function is undefined or assigned a different value there. Continuity at a point adds the requirement that the function value equal that limit. Epsilon-delta language makes this precise: every requested output tolerance can be met by choosing a sufficiently small input neighborhood. Continuity rules out finite jumps but does not guarantee a derivative; the absolute-value function is continuous at zero yet has a corner there. Limits expose removable singularities such as a cancelled factor, while one-sided limits reveal boundaries and discontinuities. In numerical software, local smoothness matters because derivative-based approximations rely on nearby inputs producing controlled output changes. Domain restrictions, branch conditions, and singular denominators must be checked before applying derivative formulas.

Appendix.title: Linear systems and fundamental subspaces
Appendix.Content: Linear systems and fundamental subspaces

A linear system <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> </mrow> </math> asks which inputs satisfy all row measurements at once. It is consistent exactly when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> </mrow> </math> lies in the column space. The null space contains input changes invisible to every measurement; rank-nullity counts observable versus free directions.
Use it when: explaining consistency, underdetermination, least squares, parameter observability, or constraints in geometry.

Developed in Phase 8: The expanded treatment connects each row to a hyperplane and the complete matrix to a map: consistency asks whether the target lies in the column space, while the null space describes every invisible change to a solution. Rank then counts constrained directions and determines the dimension of the solution family. constraint geometry · rank and solution families

Appendix.title: Mastery evidence levels
Appendix.Content: Mastery evidence levels

PROJECTALLMIGHT should not use one word such as “developed” for fundamentally different evidence states. A concept can be well explained but not executable, executable in a CPU reference but not on the native GPU, or validated in a teaching lab but not in the current production repository.
Use the following evidence ladder.
0 — Indexed
The topic has a real node, canonical name, prerequisites and destination. This proves discoverability only.
1 — Explained
The forcing problem, definitions, conventions and causal mental model are stated without relying on unexplained jargon.
2 — Derived and traced
The central mathematics or algorithm is derived with symbol meanings, assumptions and at least one nontrivial worked trace containing intermediate state.
3 — Reference implemented
A complete, rebuildable implementation exists in the teaching surface or a linked standalone laboratory. Positive and negative cases execute.
4 — Independently verified
The mechanism is checked against an oracle, invariant, property test, differential implementation, numerical bound or external normative reference strong enough to expose plausible bugs.
5 — Native-system verified

Claims involving a real API/device/tool are exercised on that system: Vulkan validation/device output, Metal GPU capture, Blender/Maya/Houdini/Nuke host execution, real filesystem semantics, real network stack, and so on.
6 — Production-repository grounded

The current Kairo/Maveb/Vulkax/Nanoquant or other target repository revision is inspected and the exact implementation, ownership, lifetime, synchronization, performance and failure paths are tied back to the lesson.
7 — Reconstructed mastery
The learner can derive, implement, trace, profile, debug and compare alternatives without copying the source, and can solve a transfer problem in a different context.

A concept can hold several evidence dimensions separately. For example, Vulkan synchronization may be Derived=Yes, CPU reference=Yes, Native Vulkan=No, Kairo parity=Unverified. Do not collapse that into one optimistic “complete” flag.
Required proof fields
For each M001–M180 chunk, the evidence ledger should record:

ListItem.Content: canonical section;
original part range;
definitions and conventions;
derivation;
worked trace;
executable/reference artifact;
positive/negative/property tests;
alternatives/failure modes;
external source review;
native platform evidence if applicable;
production repository evidence;
research bridge;
retrieval/oral reconstruction status.

Appendix.title: Matrix factorization choices
Appendix.Content: Matrix factorization choices

Choose a solver from the matrix promises and task: pivoted LU for general square systems, Cholesky for SPD systems, QR for full-rank least squares, SVD or rank-revealing methods when weak directions matter, and iterative methods for suitable large sparse workloads. Reuse factors for repeated right-hand sides.
Use it when: choosing an algorithm before implementing or calling a numerical routine.

Developed in Phase 8: The factorization should follow the matrix structure and the requested result: LU handles general square systems, Cholesky exploits positive definiteness, QR fits full-rank least squares, and SVD handles uncertain rank and spectral questions. The comparison also weighs sparsity, reuse, memory, and whether an iterative tolerance is acceptable. factorization selection · the runnable LU example

Appendix.title: Matrix functions
Appendix.Content: Matrix functions

For diagonalizable matrices, a scalar function can be applied to eigenvalues in a usable eigenbasis. Matrix exponential models linear constant-coefficient dynamics; logarithm and square root require domain and branch choices. Stable algorithms such as scaling-and-squaring are distinct from the defining power series.
Use it when: integrating linear dynamics or interpolating structured transforms.

Developed in Phase 8: A matrix function applies scalar behavior to invariant directions when the decomposition permits it, but its definition and its stable algorithm are separate. The exponential solves a linear differential equation; logarithms and square roots require domain and branch choices, and powers range from repeated multiplication to fractional transforms. matrix functions · domains and branches

Appendix.Content: Matrix multiplication and composition order

Definition and mechanism

The product AB applies B first for column-vector actions. Its entries sum A(i,k)B(k,j) over the shared dimension. Composition is associative over exact scalars and usually noncommutative; floating-point evaluation orders need not agree bitwise.
Reconstruction cue: Rotation followed by translation differs from translation followed by rotation.

Appendix.title: Matrix norms and numerical error
Appendix.Content: Matrix norms and numerical error

The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate.
Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics.

Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation
Prerequisites
Norms lengths and induced distances, Singular value decomposition, Forward and backward error.
Used by
Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, Matrix functions, Sparse and iterative solvers.
Teaching path: norms and error.
A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound

A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.

Appendix.title: Matrix transpose symmetry and trace
Appendix.Content: Matrix transpose symmetry and trace
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

Transpose exchanges row and column indices and reverses product order. Symmetric and skew-symmetric parts reconstruct any real square matrix. Trace is the diagonal sum and is invariant under similarity, while cyclic product trace needs compatible dimensions.
Reconstruction cue: (AB)T=BT A^T; real skew-symmetric matrices have zero diagonal.

Appendix.title: Minkowski sums and support mappings
Appendix.Content: Minkowski sums and support mappings
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

Minkowski addition combines pairwise position coordinates of sets in a common frame. Collision difference means <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> here. A support function returns an extreme scalar measurement; a support mapping returns a maximizing point, possibly with ties.

Intervals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> have difference <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, containing zero. Support of the difference uses a support point of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> </math> minus one of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> </math> queried in the opposite direction.

Appendix.title: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
Appendix.Content: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse

The exact SVD defines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> </math> by reciprocating every positive singular value and transposing the orthogonal factors. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </math> minimizes residual first and Euclidean solution norm among minimizers second. A numerical cutoff instead produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msubsup> <mi>A</mi> <mi>τ</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msubsup> </math>: if it discards a positive singular value, it solves a retained-rank approximation and can increase the residual of the original system. The cutoff makes the treatment of weak directions explicit.
Use it when: rectangular or rank-deficient least squares needs a minimum-norm answer.

Developed in Phase 8: The exact pseudoinverse reciprocates every positive singular value, yielding the least-squares solution with minimum Euclidean norm. A practical cutoff defines a different, truncated operator: discarding even a positive singular value can increase the residual for the original system, so the tolerance and retained rank are part of the mathematical answer. the exact pseudoinverse · truncation and regularization

Appendix.title: Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening
Appendix.Content: Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A multivariate Gaussian is determined by a mean vector and a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix. When the covariance is positive definite, its density is an elliptical bell whose principal directions are covariance eigenvectors. Cholesky factorization maps independent standard-normal samples into correlated samples; whitening applies an inverse factor to express observations in unit-variance coordinates. Singular covariance instead confines the distribution to a lower-dimensional affine subspace and has no ordinary density with respect to full-dimensional volume. Covariance transforms as AΣAᵀ under a linear map and approximately as JΣJᵀ through a nonlinear map near a reference point. These equations support sensor fusion and projected uncertainty, but a Gaussian rendering kernel is not automatically a normalized probability density or epistemic uncertainty model.

Appendix.title: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization
Appendix.Content: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more.

Appendix.title: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
Appendix.source: Concepts/Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt.md
Appendix.Content: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct.

Appendix.title: Norms lengths and induced distances
Appendix.Content: Norms lengths and induced distances
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

A norm is nonnegative, definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. It induces distance by taking the norm of a point difference. Coordinate-defined first, second and infinity norms answer different geometric questions.

For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the three norms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>7</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>5</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Squared length scales quadratically and is not itself a norm or induced metric.

Appendix.title: Numerical quadrature and error
Appendix.Content: Numerical quadrature and error
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

Quadrature approximates a definite integral from finitely many function evaluations. Left, right, and midpoint rectangle rules use constant local models; the trapezoid rule uses linear interpolation; Simpson’s rule integrates a local quadratic fit over paired intervals. Their errors depend on smoothness, interval size, and rule-specific derivative bounds. Refining the mesh usually improves accuracy for smooth functions, but increases computation and may expose floating-point accumulation error. Adaptive quadrature places more samples where the integrand changes rapidly, provided its error estimator is trustworthy. Quadrature differs from Monte Carlo: deterministic rules have dimension-dependent behavior, while random sampling is attractive in high dimensions but has statistical uncertainty. Report the interval, nodes, weights, stopping tolerance, and error-control method so numerical results can be reproduced.

Appendix.title: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Appendix.Content: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory.

Appendix.title: Off-axis stereo projection and disparity
Appendix.Content: Off-axis stereo projection and disparity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Stereo cameras use two eye centres separated by a baseline, while each projection frustum is shifted so a chosen zero-parallax plane aligns in the images. Parallel eye orientations with asymmetric frusta avoid the vertical mismatch and discomfort often introduced by toe-in cameras. For rectified pinhole cameras, disparity is approximately <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>Z</mi> </math>, so inferred depth is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math> under the calibration and rectification assumptions. Depth uncertainty grows roughly with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>Z</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> for fixed pixel disparity error. Distinguish interpupillary distance from lens and display-centre spacing; the rendered baseline is an optical/comfort design decision. Use consistent pixel units for focal length, baseline, and disparity before computing metric depth.

Appendix.title: Omnidirectional camera projections
Appendix.Content: Omnidirectional camera projections
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Cubemaps, equirectangular panoramas, and fisheye lenses map unit directions onto different image domains. A cubemap selects one of six faces and projects two direction components; equirectangular coordinates map longitude and latitude to a rectangle; fisheye mappings use a radial function of angular distance. These parameterizations are not equal-area: uniform pixel sampling does not imply uniform solid-angle sampling. Choose the mapping that matches capture or rendering needs, define face orientation and seam rules, and measure reconstruction with angular error between unit vectors. Fisheye formulas also differ (equidistant, equisolid, orthographic, stereographic), so name the model before interpreting pixels. At the poles, longitude is undefined, so seam and pole handling need explicit sampling rules.

Appendix.title: Online moments and Welford accumulation
Appendix.Content: Online moments and Welford accumulation
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Online statistics update a mean and centered sum of squares as observations arrive, using constant storage. Welford’s recurrence computes a new mean from the old mean and one sample, then adds the product of deviations measured before and after that update. The centered form avoids severe cancellation in E[X²]−E[X]² for data with a large offset and small spread. Divide accumulated scatter by n for descriptive population-normalized variance or by n−1 for unbiased sample variance under IID finite-variance assumptions. The recurrence is numerically better behaved, not immune to overflow, count exhaustion, or all rounding error. Parallel workers can merge count, mean, and scatter summaries with a correction term for different means; merge order can change floating-point results.

Appendix.title: Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
Appendix.Content: Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6
Definition and mechanism

An orthonormal frame has unit perpendicular axes, so its Gram matrix is identity. Gram–Schmidt constructs axes by repeated rejection. Modified order uses the updated residual and changes rounding behavior. Frame existence, numerical reliability and output continuity are distinct questions.

For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, rejection produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A least-aligned helper axis avoids a near-parallel cross but can switch discontinuously.

Appendix.title: PCA and covariance eigensystems
Appendix.Content: PCA and covariance eigensystems

Center sample rows, then find the orthogonal directions of greatest variance. For centered <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>, SVD gives directions in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>, scores in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> </math>, and covariance eigenvalues <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msubsup> <mi>σ</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Units and feature scaling change the question; near-equal eigenvalues make individual axes unstable.
Use it when: describing point clouds, reducing dimensions, or estimating a best-fit plane.

Developed in Phase 8: PCA first centers observations so the covariance measures variation around the sample mean. The right singular vectors of centered data give principal directions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> </math> gives scores, and squared singular values scaled by sample count give covariance eigenvalues; feature units and small eigengaps affect interpretation. centering and principal axes · plane fits and eigengaps

Phase 9–10 development: For a random vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math> with finite second moments, covariance is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. For every vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>≥</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, so covariance is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvectors give uncorrelated principal directions and the eigenvalues give variance along them. Whitening rescales nonzero-variance directions and needs a stated policy for zero or tiny eigenvalues. A Gaussian kernel used to model rendering footprints is a spatial distribution model, not automatically a statement about epistemic uncertainty.
Prerequisites

Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Singular value decomposition, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky. - Expectation, covariance, and dependence - Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening - Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse - QR factorization and least squares

Appendix.title: Polar decomposition
Appendix.Content: Polar decomposition

The right polar form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>H</mi> </math> separates an orthogonal factor from a positive-semidefinite stretch <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>H</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>A</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. The orthogonal factor may include reflection; singular matrices can make its completion nonunique. Symmetric stretch can include shear in the chosen coordinates.
Use it when: separating local rigid-like motion from symmetric deformation.

Developed in Phase 8: Polar decomposition factors a map into an orthogonal part and a positive-semidefinite stretch. The SVD constructs both left and right forms, separates reflection from a proper rotation, and gives the nearest orthogonal or special-orthogonal factor when the singular directions allow a unique choice; zero singular values leave completion freedom. left and right stretch · nearest proper rotation and ambiguity

Singular value decomposition, Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Determinants orientation and volume.

Appendix.title: Position reconstruction from depth
Appendix.Content: Position reconstruction from depth
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11
Definition and mechanism

Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset.

Appendix.title: Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
Appendix.Content: Probability spaces, events, and conditioning
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A probability model consists of a sample space, a collection of measurable events, and a probability measure assigning values to those events. Conditional probability renormalizes the measure within an event of positive probability; Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning by combining likelihood with prior probability. Independence is a factorization property, not a synonym for disjointness or zero correlation. Conditioning on a zero-probability event cannot use the ordinary ratio directly; continuous models need density-based or regular conditional formulations. This framework keeps possible outcomes separate from distributions placed on them and clarifies what information an experiment provides. A random model can describe a deterministic pseudorandom generator over a distribution of seeds, but one fixed seed produces a fixed sequence. State the event model and conditioning assumptions before interpreting probability as evidence.
