This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals — Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism A reduced rational p/q terminates in base B iff q divides a power of B. In binary q must be a power of two. Binary32 0.1 is exactly 13421773/2^27, chosen as an approximation of non-dyadic 1/10. Prerequisites
Positional notation — Finite fractional digits correspond to an integer over a power of the base. Binary32 — Its finite significand/exponent makes each stored finite value a dyadic rational.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid. Pending: Other bases, decimal conversion algorithms and exact rational arithmetic. Source and navigation M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Why decimal-friendly numbers can be binary-hostile A reduced rational number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </math> has a terminating representation in base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> exactly when every prime factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> also divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math>. Base 10 has prime factors 2 and 5, so fractions such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>10</mn> </math> terminate. Base 2 has only prime factor 2, so only dyadic rationals with denominator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>k</mi> </msup> </math> terminate. That is why <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.25</mn> </math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.125</mn> </math> are exact in ordinary binary floating point while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.1</mn> </math> repeats forever and must be rounded. The issue is not that floating point is “bad at decimals”; it is a consequence of positional representation. This perspective helps debugging: multiplying a binary approximation to 0.1 by ten need not recreate the exact path one imagines from decimal arithmetic. For currency or protocol fields whose semantics are decimal-exact, scaled integers or decimal floating formats may be better contracts. A reconstruction exercise should reduce several fractions, classify their denominator prime factors, and predict whether they terminate in bases 2, 10, and 16 before checking actual floating encodings.. Open Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Latent-variable models and generative flows — Latent-variable models and generative flows Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Generative models describe how data could be produced, often by first sampling a latent variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> </math> and mapping it to an observation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>. A variational autoencoder (VAE) learns an encoder distribution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and decoder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; its evidence lower bound balances reconstruction likelihood against a KL penalty that keeps the latent distribution tractable. A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a discriminator, creating a game that can produce sharp samples but may be unstable or collapse to limited modes. Normalizing flows use invertible transformations so the data density can be computed with a change-of-variables Jacobian determinant. These methods solve different tradeoffs among likelihood, sample quality, latent structure, and optimization stability. Their assumptions matter: a VAE’s posterior family may be too simple, a GAN score is not a calibrated density, and a flow’s invertibility constrains architecture. Generated samples are not evidence that the model has learned the true causal process. Prerequisites
Probability density and change of measure Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Research validity and ablation Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Used by
Generative models learn distributions and samplers Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting
Full teaching explanation

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Rendering history validity — Rendering history validity A temporal renderer reuses information from earlier frames only if that information still estimates the same target quantity at the reprojected location. “Previous frame exists” is therefore not enough. History needs a validity contract. A history sample may become invalid because of:
camera cuts or projection changes; resize or dynamic-resolution changes; object transform discontinuities; newly visible or disoccluded surfaces; material or lighting changes; estimator changes such as sample pattern, exposure domain or denoiser configuration; resource reallocation or version replacement.
Reprojection is a hypothesis Motion vectors or previous transforms propose a correspondence from current sample to previous sample. The renderer should test that hypothesis with available evidence such as depth, normal, object/material identity, velocity magnitude or neighborhood statistics. A common failure is using a valid coordinate that points to the wrong surface. Bounds checking prevents memory errors, not temporal ghosting. Versioned history Treat history like a cache with a key. Relevant state changes advance a version or invalidate specific history resources. The render graph can then express that a temporal pass consumes history version N and produces version N+1. This is also important for progressive path tracing. Accumulation belongs to a camera/scene/material/light/estimator state. If any target-defining state changes and old samples remain, the output converges to a mixture of different images. Failure-oriented tests Useful temporal tests include a hard camera cut, a moving foreground object revealing background, an emissive material changing abruptly, resize, FOV change, jitter-sequence restart, and an object whose ID remains but geometry changes. For each case, record which history samples should survive and why. The existing render-graph witness proves logical resource dependencies, not temporal validity itself. Native renderer evidence should capture motion/depth/ID buffers and show the acceptance/rejection mask. Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership. Related: Temporal reprojection and history validation, Reversed-Z depth contracts.. Open Rendering history validity in Volume 2

A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Numerical error budgets — Numerical error budgets Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A computed result can differ from a target because of model assumptions, discretization, solver termination, arithmetic, sampling, or uncertain reference data. These contributions may interact, so an additive budget is a diagnostic model rather than a universal identity. First identify which errors are deterministic bounds, which are observed estimates, and which are stochastic uncertainty. For example, a ray-traced pixel can combine approximation of geometry, finite sample variance, floating-point accumulation, and an imperfect reference image. Allocate effort where the dominant contribution lies: extra precision cannot fix model bias, and more samples cannot repair an incorrect PDF. Report units and assumptions with every tolerance. Prerequisites
Forward and backward error Conditioning and singularity Algorithmic stability Discretization, truncation, and roundoff Bracketed and open root solvers A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation Position reconstruction from depth
Used by
Reproducible numerical benchmarking
Full teaching explanation

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Guest and host integer domains — Guest and host integer domains Curriculum depth: Forward · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism An emulator may compute an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit guest operation in a wider host type so carry and other discarded architectural information remain observable. Guest means the machine being emulated; host means the implementation platform. An eight-bit guest addition can use a host temporary holding 0–511, extract carry, then narrow to 0–255. Host signed overflow must never be used to imitate guest wrap. Prerequisites
Fixed-width integer types — When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags — For eight-bit addition, C tests exact sum>255; V tests signed sum outside [−128,127]; N is result bit 7; Z tests low result==0.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: IEEE-754 floating point — IEEE-754 floating point Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism IEEE-754 specifies floating formats and behavior including representation classes, rounding directions and exception conditions. A finite bit pattern is interpreted through sign, exponent and significand rules, not as a two’s-complement integer. Binary32 has 1/8/23 stored fields and 24-bit normal precision; binary64 has 1/11/52 fields and 53-bit normal precision. Word 412A0000 encodes 10.625 in binary32. Exponent-zero and all-one fields distinguish zero/subnormal and infinity/NaN. Normal spacing expands with exponent; nearest-even and directed modes choose representable results under explicit rules. These format names do not prove every C++ float/double has those representations. M005 develops alignment, cancellation, FMA and accumulated error. Numeric equality is not representation identity, and moving rounding points can change the computed result. Prerequisites
Bit field — A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member. Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.
Used by
Binary16 — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Bfloat16 — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Fused multiply-add — Fused operation semantics and destination rounding are part of the arithmetic contract. Binary32 — uses ieee-754 floating point to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy. Floating-point exception flags — uses ieee-754 floating point to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy. Bit casting and representation — uses ieee-754 floating point to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy. Robust norm and intermediate range — uses ieee-754 floating point to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy.
Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Binary16 — Binary16 Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism IEEE binary16 has 1/5/10 fields, bias15 and11 normal precision bits. Word3E00 is1.5; maximum finite65504; normal minimum2^-14 and subnormal minimum2^-24. Prerequisites
IEEE-754 floating point — supplies the representation or validity rule used above. Rounding to nearest ties to even — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Actual GPU arithmetic and conversion support are not tested by the scalar codec. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth IEEE binary16 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits and 10 stored fraction bits. Normal numbers have an implicit leading one, giving 11 bits of significand precision. The narrow exponent and significand make half precision cheaper to store and move than binary32, but not a drop-in replacement for every intermediate. Around magnitude 1, adjacent normal values are roughly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> apart. As magnitude grows, spacing grows with the exponent. Subnormals extend representable values toward zero with reduced precision, while exponent all-ones encodes infinities and NaNs. A graphics or ML pipeline should distinguish storage precision from accumulation precision. Vertex attributes, textures or weights may be stored as binary16 while dot products and reductions accumulate in binary32. This often preserves bandwidth savings without accepting catastrophic accumulation error. Tests should include exact endpoints around 1, overflow to infinity according to conversion rules, underflow and subnormals, signed zero and NaN propagation policy. Hardware may flush subnormals or use mixed-precision instructions, so performance behavior requires target-specific evidence.. Open Binary16 in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Bit casting and representation — Bit casting and representation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation. M006 separates representation copying, numeric conversion and endian coding. Eligibility does not validate arbitrary padding/target representations or establish a typed object in file-mapped bytes. Use initialized compatible scalars and explicit external encoding. Prerequisites
Fixed-width integer types — A same-size unsigned carrier holds the specified interchange representation. Interpretation contract — A bit transfer and a numeric conversion interpret the same carrier differently. IEEE-754 floating point — The format/arithmetic contract gives these bits their numerical domain.
Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Edge localization and subpixel contours — Edge localization and subpixel contours Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism An edge is a rapid image-intensity change, often associated with a material or depth boundary. Differentiating a noisy image amplifies high-frequency noise, so edge detectors first smooth with a Gaussian-like filter and then compute a gradient. Gradient magnitude estimates edge strength; gradient direction estimates the local normal. Nonmaximum suppression keeps a candidate only if it is a local maximum along that normal, thinning a broad response to a contour. Thresholding and hysteresis connect strong responses through weaker neighboring pixels. Subpixel localization fits a local peak to gradient samples, estimating a contour position between pixel centers. Accuracy depends on sampling, blur, contrast, and the assumed edge profile. This makes edge detection a measurement problem whose output uncertainty should propagate into later line, pose, or shape fitting. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Sampling aliasing and reconstruction
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Hough transform and geometric voting Template matching and distance transforms
Full teaching explanation Edges, contours, and subpixel localization · Recognition, templates, and industrial matching. Open Edge localization and subpixel contours in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Little endian — Little endian Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism The lowest address holds the least-significant octet. For 0x12345678, offsets 0–3 hold 78/56/34/12. Writer byte i selects bits 8i through 8i+7; a matching reader restores the same weights. This is byte order, not bit reversal. Prerequisites
Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions. Shift operations — Shifts relocate a selected byte or address field to its significance position.
Used by Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept. Recall and next depth Write and decode four bytes, including leading zero bytes. Pending: Mixed-endian cases and protocol integration. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth Little-endian byte order stores the least-significant byte first. The 32-bit integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>12345678</mn> </math> appears in increasing memory addresses as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>78</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>56</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>34</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>12.</mn> </math> That layout is useful only after the interpretation contract is known: the same four bytes could be part of an integer, float, packed header or text. Endianness never supplies the type by itself. Most contemporary desktop CPUs are little-endian, but that is not permission to encode a durable binary format with raw object bytes. A format needs explicit field widths, byte order, versioning and bounds checks. If a file is defined little-endian, decode each field as little-endian even on a little-endian host; the explicit operation documents the contract and preserves portability. Tests should use byte arrays whose numeric values are obvious, include unaligned offsets, and verify both read and write paths. For floating point, byte order and IEEE-754 representation are separate assumptions.. Open Little endian in Volume 1

A const int& bound to an int lvalue tracks that integer; a const double& initialized from the same int binds a converted temporary snapshot. Base-subobject binding need not copy; bit-fields cannot provide ordinary mutable integer references. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Machine epsilon — Machine epsilon Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold. Prerequisites
Significand and hidden bit — Fraction weights and effective precision determine value and the smallest retained position.
Used by
ULP and representable spacing — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Numerical tolerance policies — uses this mechanism in its explanation.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the concrete example in the definition and identify its validity assumptions. Pending: Explain min, denorm_min, lowest, and task-specific tolerance independently. Source and navigation M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map Epsilon is local to one magnitude For a floating type, machine epsilon is commonly defined as the distance from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math> to the next representable number greater than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>. For binary precision <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math>, that spacing is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>. It describes one location in the representable lattice; it is not a universal comparison tolerance. Floating spacing scales with exponent. Near a large world coordinate, one ULP can be much larger than epsilon; near zero, subnormal spacing follows a different regime. Therefore testing abs(a-b) < epsilon for arbitrary geometric or physical quantities is usually unjustified. A defensible comparison begins with the domain: absolute tolerance for quantities near zero, relative tolerance when scale matters, ULP bounds when representation-level proximity is intended, or an exact predicate when the algorithm can provide one. Tests should include values near 1, large magnitudes, tiny normals/subnormals and adjacent representable values using nextafter.. Open Machine epsilon in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Saturating arithmetic — Saturating arithmetic Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Clamp unrepresentable results to range boundaries instead of wrapping; useful for bounded media values but generally non-associative. Saturation clamps a mathematical result to a permitted interval: unsigned-byte 250+20 becomes 255 instead of 14. Clamp a widened result. Signed saturation is not associative: saturating (100+100)−100 yields 27 while 100+saturating(100−100) yields 100. Prerequisites
Arithmetic policies — A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision. Signed integer overflow — Overflow concerns the operation’s signed type after promotions.
Used by Connect later chunks here when they use this concept. Recall and next depth Explain saturating arithmetic without the label, work the example above, then state the assumption whose removal would change the result. Pending: SIMD saturation, normalized formats, HDR policy, and evaluation-order effects. Source and navigation C002 teaching chapter · Part definitions and mechanisms · Dependency Map. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Sterbenz lemma — Sterbenz lemma Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism For nonnegative stored radix-format floats x,y with x/2≤y≤2x, the difference is representable exactly under appropriate gradual-underflow assumptions. This does not recover errors already present in the operands. Prerequisites
Cancellation and loss of significance — Near-equal operand errors motivate exact-subtraction distinctions and reformulation. Subnormals and gradual underflow — An exact tiny difference may need gradual-underflow representability.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid. Pending: Prove range/significand details for a chosen format; FTZ changes assumptions. Source and navigation M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Exact subtraction in a bounded ratio Sterbenz’s lemma gives a rare exactness guarantee for floating subtraction. Under the usual floating-point assumptions, if two finite floating values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>y</mi> </math> satisfy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mfrac> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>≤</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> </math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>y</mi> </math> is exactly representable in the same floating format, provided the result remains in the supported range conditions. This explains why cancellation is not synonymous with rounding error. Subtracting two nearby floating numbers can lose relative information about the original quantities, yet the subtraction operation itself may be exact. The conditioning of the problem and the rounding of an operation are different questions. The lemma is useful when proving error bounds for compensated algorithms and geometric predicates. A reconstruction test should generate representable pairs inside and outside the ratio interval, compare the subtraction against a higher-precision exact reference, and distinguish an exactly rounded zero/small difference from a well-conditioned final answer.. Open Sterbenz lemma in Volume 1

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Signed zero — Signed zero Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero. Prerequisites
Binary32 — The concrete fields provide the representation used in this mechanism.
Used by
ULP distance policies — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Floating-point canonicalization — uses this mechanism in its explanation.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the concrete example in the definition and identify its validity assumptions. Pending: Specify zero equality separately from raw-byte equality and ULP ordering. Source and navigation M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth IEEE-754 has both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. They compare equal numerically in ordinary equality, but the sign remains observable through operations such as reciprocal, sign-bit inspection and some branch-cut-sensitive functions: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> Signed zero preserves directional information after underflow or exact cancellation. That can matter in complex functions, interval boundaries and geometric code that interprets the sign of a quantity near a separating surface. It can also surprise serialization, hashing and deterministic comparison. If the application’s semantic model says both zeros are identical, canonicalization may deliberately map negative zero to positive zero before hashing or bytewise equality. If directional zero is meaningful, that canonicalization destroys information. Tests should distinguish numeric equality from bit representation and include operations that expose the sign. This is one reason floating-point equality policy must start from domain semantics rather than from a universal epsilon.. Open Signed zero in Volume 1

Relative error divides by nonzero reference magnitude and is dimensionless; it is undefined at true zero. A 1e-12 absolute error can be 100% of a 1e-12 value. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Exceptional projections and dimension — Exceptional projections and dimension Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>, count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>θ</mi> </math>; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension Projection rejection and scalar components Fourier analysis and spectral phase Vector spaces subspaces and span
Used by
Finite-field projections turn image size into collision counts Real projections add scale, spacing, and incidence geometry Additive energy and approximate structure

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Camera calibration and bundle adjustment — Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Camera calibration estimates parameters that map 3D points to image coordinates. Intrinsics describe focal scale, principal point, and lens distortion; extrinsics describe camera pose relative to the scene. Known calibration targets provide 3D-to-2D correspondences, and a nonlinear least-squares objective minimizes reprojection error. Bundle adjustment jointly refines many camera poses and 3D feature points by minimizing all observed image residuals. The problem is sparse because each image sees only a subset of points. It also has gauge freedoms: translating or scaling the entire reconstruction may leave projections unchanged, so fix a reference pose or scale. Robust loss functions reduce the effect of mismatched features. Good initialization, parameter scaling, and Jacobian structure determine whether optimization converges. Prerequisites
Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Singular value decomposition
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Stereo correspondence and epipolar geometry Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting Off-axis stereo projection and disparity Omnidirectional camera projections Position reconstruction from depth Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Full teaching explanation Cameras, projection, and calibration · Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Stereo, relative orientation, and reconstruction Phase 11 camera development Linearize reprojection residuals as r(θ+δ)≈r(θ)+Jδ; the weighted information matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>J</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>W</mi> <mi>J</mi> </math> reveals parameter combinations that change observations. Null directions are local ambiguities, while small eigenvalues indicate weak constraints. In calibrated monocular structure from motion, global frame choice and common scene scale are gauge freedoms. Fix a pose and scale convention, or add a metric measurement, before interpreting covariance. Repeated nearly identical views may leave focal length, depth, and pose coupled even with many pixels. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Camera calibration and bundle adjustment in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Named members versus array elements — Named members versus array elements Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism The x member’s one-past pointer is not an authorized y access. A span describes an already-valid range; adjacency cannot create that range. Adjacent x/y/z fields are separate subobjects, not T[3]. A pointer to x supports one-element-array pointer arithmetic; one-past cannot be dereferenced to access y. span(&x,3) does not create an array. Use explicit member dispatch or actual array storage; a ToArray result is a copy. Prerequisites
Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Array-relative pointer bounds explain why adjacency of separate members cannot authorize indexing.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation — Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism After a vertex is transformed, its clip-space coordinate is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Clip primitives against the view volume before perspective division; under the conventional OpenGL clip convention the inequalities are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math>. A crossing edge is split by interpolating its homogeneous endpoints, which preserves the projective line and avoids dividing by a small or negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math> too early. Only surviving points are divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msub> </math> to enter normalized device coordinates. Attributes then need perspective-correct interpolation: screen-space barycentric weights interpolate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>w</mi> </math>, and the fragment value is their ratio. For a triangle with weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Direct linear interpolation in screen space is correct only for affine quantities or equal depth; otherwise textures warp. Clip-space depth conventions and the near/far interval vary by API and projection setup, so the inequalities must match the active pipeline. Prerequisites
Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Camera view and clip-space pipeline Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Depth buffering and visibility order GPU vertex specification
Used by

Full teaching explanation
Rasterization, coverage, and depth Cameras, projection, and calibration

Derive the clip-space edge intersection and perspective-correct attribute ratio. Why must clipping happen before divide by w, and why is linear screen interpolation wrong for texture coordinates?
Source and navigation Teaching narrative: open the main explanation. Browse the University graphics and vision index. Additional chapter connections: Cameras, projection, and calibration; Rasterization, coverage, and depth; Homogeneous coordinates preserve the role of a location; A camera is another frame, so viewing uses its inverse. Caption/source records: P1-02, P3-05, P3-06, P3-12. Phase 11 camera development Clipping and perspective-correct interpolation preserve projective geometry, while texture filtering asks how much surface area maps to a pixel. Neighboring camera rays approximate the image-to-surface footprint. At grazing angles one pixel can cover a long, thin region; a center-only texel lookup may alias detail even when attributes interpolate correctly. Use footprint estimates to select mip levels or anisotropic filters, while respecting visibility edges where derivatives jump. Ray differentials aid sampling but do not replace clipping or multisample coverage. Source basis: PBRT differential-ray texture filtering. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review. Worked clip-plane trace beside the shader explanation For clip endpoints <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the right-plane intersection uses homogeneous edge parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>5</mn> </math>; interpolating the already divided endpoints would use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math>. The worked trace and pipeline figure also explain negative fourth components, the zero-divisor limit and declared depth conventions. This is used by the shader-stage teaching before program compilation and linking are discussed. Executable raster-state continuation The project now carries two complementary CPU witnesses. tools/labs/raster_reference_lab.cpp owns edge coverage, barycentrics, perspective-correct interpolation and depth ordering. tools/labs/raster_pipeline_state_lab.cpp continues the same pipeline through a homogeneous clip-plane intersection, an explicit four-sample coverage mask, stencil compare/pass update and premultiplied source-over blending. That separation is deliberate: clipping happens in homogeneous coordinates before divide-by-<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math>; sample ownership happens after screen mapping; stencil/depth are stateful per-fragment/sample decisions; blending combines a surviving source with an existing destination. Treating all of them as “rasterization” without preserving these boundaries makes debugging nearly impossible.. Open Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation — Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method. Phase 9–10 development Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration. Prerequisites
Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Matrix multiplication and composition order Floating-point reassociation Derivative as a local linear map Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Antialiasing and sample allocation — Antialiasing and sample allocation Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies. Phase 9–10 development Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space. Prerequisites
Sampling aliasing and reconstruction — Allocation/filtering must respect what reduced samples can distinguish. Multiscale texture filtering — Coarse samples need appropriate prefilter/footprint representations. Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise
Used by
Temporal reprojection and history validation

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Integral promotion — Integral promotion Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Narrow integral operands promote to int when it represents their entire range, otherwise to unsigned int; the operator acts at that promoted width. Narrow integer types become int if int represents every original value; otherwise they become unsigned int. Promotion happens before the operation, not only on assignment. On the usual host, uint8_t{250}+uint8_t{10} is int 260; converting afterward to uint8_t yields 4. Prerequisites
Fixed-width integer types — When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms — Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Phase 7 derives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mi>S</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>R</mi> <msup> <mi>S</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> for orthogonal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math> and nonzero diagonal scales <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>S</mi> </math>, explains why zero scale invalidates inverse-based normal transport, and distinguishes shading-normal direction from determinant-signed cross-derived area. TRS normal derivation. A covector is a linear scalar-valued measurement rule. Surface normals represent rules annihilating tangent movement. Under an invertible active linear transform, preserved measurements require inverse-transpose normal transformation. A metric identifies vector and covector representations. For tangent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, doubling horizontal scale requires normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> to preserve perpendicularity. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension — An ordered basis fixes coordinate meaning and the space whose geometry is measured. Dot products and orthogonality — Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.
Used by Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Ray-triangle intersection — Ray-triangle intersection Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A ray is a parametric half-line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>o</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mi>d</mi> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>o</mi> </math> is its origin, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>d</mi> </math> is its direction, and only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>≥</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> lies ahead of the ray. To intersect a triangle, first intersect the ray with its plane, then express the hit point in barycentric coordinates and accept it only if the weights lie inside the triangle. An equivalent determinant test solves for ray distance and two barycentric coordinates together. The hit record should state whether the result is nearest, any, or all intersections; those are different query contracts. Parallel or nearly parallel rays, degenerate triangles, and hits near edges require care because small floating-point errors can change classification. Scale-aware tolerances and consistent orientation predicates reduce cracks and self-intersection artifacts. Prerequisites
Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Learned image features and CNNs — Learned image features and CNNs Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A convolutional neural network (CNN) learns filters that detect useful image patterns from data. A convolution layer applies the same small kernel at many image locations, so a feature such as an edge can be recognized wherever it appears. Early layers often respond to local contrast or texture; later layers combine these responses into task-specific patterns. Stride and pooling reduce spatial resolution, trading detail for computation and larger receptive fields. Training adjusts filter values by gradient descent using backpropagation and labeled or self-supervised objectives. Weight sharing gives translation equivariance: shifting an input shifts the feature map, but does not guarantee full translation invariance or robustness to scale, viewpoint, lighting, or distribution change. Padding and stride determine border behavior and output size; too much downsampling can erase small objects. A learned feature is a representation useful for a training objective, not a human-interpretable semantic guarantee. Performance depends on data coverage, augmentation, architecture, optimization, and honest held-out evaluation. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Research validity and ablation Retinal encoding and receptive fields Automatic differentiation and backpropagation
Used by
Convolutional models preserve image neighborhoods Attention and visual transformers Contrastive vision and image-language alignment Perception feedback and robot learning
Full teaching explanation
Convolutional models preserve image neighborhoods
Recall and next depth
Follow how one shared kernel creates a feature map and how stride changes its resolution. What property does convolution provide under translation, and what transformations does it not make invariant?

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Probability density and change of measure — Probability density and change of measure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over area differs from a density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>ω</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>ω</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math> in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration. Phase 9–10 development A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability. Prerequisites
Light spectra and radiometry Random variables and probability laws

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: One Definition Rule — One Definition Rule Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C007 Definition and mechanism ODR requires coherent definitions. A non-inline externally linked function normally needs one program definition when odr-used. Certain class, template and inline definitions can appear in multiple translation units only under the rule’s conditions, including matching tokens and lookup; named-module attachment changes the permitted cases. Header guards operate within one translation unit, not across the program. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Deterministic reduction tree — Deterministic reduction tree Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism A reduction fixes input order, partition and merge topology so scheduling cannot change the arithmetic grouping. Midpoint recursive splitting is one such tree. Different SIMD widths or partitions can otherwise change it. Prerequisites
Compensated and pairwise summation — A fixed pairwise topology specifies the additions a deterministic reduction performs.
Used by
Numerical reproducibility — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid. Pending: Cross-platform identity also requires compatible operation semantics, precision, libraries and environment. Source and navigation M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel reduction can change low bits when thread count, work partition or scheduling changes. A deterministic reduction tree fixes grouping order independently of which worker finishes first. For eight values, a balanced tree can always compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>5</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>6</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>7</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The balanced tree can also reduce error growth compared with some highly unbalanced orders, although it is not equivalent to exact or compensated summation. Determinism costs constraints: the implementation may need stable chunk boundaries, temporary partials and an ordered merge. On GPUs, subgroup width and dispatch shape can otherwise change the effective tree. Tests should permute scheduling while preserving logical indices and require identical result bits for the deterministic path. A separate accuracy test should compare against a higher-precision or compensated reference; repeatability and numerical accuracy are related but distinct properties.. Open Deterministic reduction tree in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: One-bit centroid quantization — One-bit centroid quantization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row. Prerequisites
Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Empty-side, zero and non-finite policies must be explicit in a production codec. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth One-bit centroid quantization does not merely store a sign. A group of source values is partitioned into two reconstruction levels, often centroids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math>, and each element stores one membership bit. Decoding is therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> If the centroids are fixed to symmetric values such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>, metadata becomes cheaper but the representation loses the ability to follow asymmetric distributions. If they are fitted per group, metadata cost increases but reconstruction error can fall. The useful engineering quantity is total cost, not bits-per-weight in isolation: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mtext>effective bits/value</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mtext>centroid metadata bits</mtext> <mtext>group size</mtext> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> Small groups adapt better but pay more metadata and may reduce SIMD efficiency. Large groups amortize metadata but force unrelated values to share two reconstruction levels. A correct implementation tests deterministic centroid selection, empty-cluster handling, tie policy, bit packing order, group tails, finite decoded values, and error against a declared metric. For inference, the important next question is whether the binary code can participate directly in a dot-product kernel or must be expanded first; that determines whether compression actually saves bandwidth.. Open One-bit centroid quantization in Volume 1

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Two's complement — Two’s complement Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math> is residue <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=∼</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>; the signed high-bit weight is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, giving one zero and an asymmetric range. For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ. Thus 0xAD means 173−256=−83. Negation uses width-limited complement plus one modulo 2ᴺ. Signed interpretation and unsigned residue share bits but have different language arithmetic contracts. Prerequisites
Unsigned modular arithmetic — Modulo m retains the remainder class after division by m. Bitwise NOT — Complement must specify width: eight-bit complement of 0x0F is 0xF0, while sixteen-bit complement is 0xFFF0.
Used by
Fixed-point representation — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Minimum signed value — uses two’s complement as part of its representation or reasoning. Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags — uses two’s complement as part of its representation or reasoning. Subtraction through addition — uses two’s complement as part of its representation or reasoning. Arithmetic policies — uses two’s complement as part of its representation or reasoning.
Recall and next depth Explain two’s complement without the label, work the example above, then state the assumption whose removal would change the result. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Binary32 — Binary32 Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism A 32-bit binary interchange format with one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. Normal precision is 24 bits; exponent bias is 127. Word 3F800000 has E=127,F=0 and means 1. Prerequisites

Mixed-precision state updates — Its finite significand/exponent makes each stored finite value a dyadic rational. Binary64 — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Exponent bias — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Significand and hidden bit — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Signed zero — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Floating-point infinities — uses this mechanism in its explanation. NaNs and payloads — uses this mechanism in its explanation.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Binary64 — Binary64 Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1. Prerequisites
Binary32 — The concrete fields provide the representation used in this mechanism.
Used by
Mixed-precision state updates — A wider format can represent finite binary32 values exactly but not recover earlier loss.
Connect later dependent concepts here as their lessons arrive. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the concrete example in the definition and identify its validity assumptions. Pending: Apply the class rules using exponent 2047; long double is not automatically this format. Source and navigation M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map Precision, exponent range, and the integer-exact region IEEE-754 binary64 uses 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 stored fraction bits. Normal values have an implicit leading one, giving 53 bits of significand precision. Around magnitude one, the gap between adjacent values is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>52</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Every integer with magnitude up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>53</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> is exactly representable, but beyond that boundary adjacent integers begin sharing the same floating representation. This matters when timestamps, IDs, byte counts or large counters are moved through a double-based API: an integer may be within the exponent range yet still lose unit precision. Binary64 dramatically reduces rounding error compared with binary32 but doubles storage/bandwidth and does not cure unstable algorithms. Coordinate systems for large worlds often use double on the CPU and camera-relative float on the GPU, making the conversion boundary part of the design. Tests should cover adjacent values around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>53</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, normal/subnormal transitions, overflow, signed zero, infinities/NaNs, and cancellation cases that remain ill-conditioned even at 64-bit precision.. Open Binary64 in Volume 1

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism std::unique_ptr<T, D> is a move-only exclusive owner whose deleter D defines disposal. get() exposes a borrow; release() transfers the responsibility without deleting. std::shared_ptr<T> joins a shared ownership group represented by a control block; the managed object is destroyed when the last strong owner is released. The control block can outlive the object while weak observers remain. The stored pointer and the object whose destruction the control block arranges can differ (for example, aliasing ownership). Shared ownership is not pointee synchronization. Concurrent operations on distinct smart-pointer handles do not automatically make concurrent access to T safe. Use sharing only when several independent parties truly retain the same lifetime. Prerequisites
Ownership and non-owning views — Access-only views and ownership responsibilities are different contracts. RAII and resource handles — Smart pointers are standard resource owners built around lifetime-bound cleanup.
Used by
Weak observation and ownership cycles Placement construction and explicit lifetime management
Recall and next depth Explain why unique_ptr<Derived> converted to unique_ptr<Base> needs a valid base destruction policy. Pending: allocator/deleter state and atomic shared ownership interfaces. Source and navigation M010 teaching narrative · Source coverage. Open Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Quantization error metrics — Quantization error metrics Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double. Prerequisites
Absolute and relative error — supplies the representation or validity rule used above. Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Representation error alone does not establish downstream task correctness. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map A metric must match what the consumer loses Quantization error is the difference <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> </math> between source and reconstruction, but one scalar summary cannot answer every engineering question. Mean squared error emphasizes large deviations; mean absolute error is less sensitive to outliers; maximum absolute error exposes worst-case bounds; relative error becomes useful when scale varies but is unstable near zero. For tensors, per-tensor MSE can hide one badly damaged channel or group. Diagnostics should often include per-group distributions, saturation counts, scale histograms, and downstream task error. A quantizer that minimizes weight MSE is not guaranteed to minimize model-output error because layers amplify directions differently. Signal metrics also depend on representation. Comparing gamma-encoded RGB with ordinary squared error is not the same as comparing linear-light energy. Normals may need angular error rather than component MSE. A useful quantization benchmark therefore reports storage cost together with several reconstruction metrics and one consumer-level metric. The metric is part of the experiment hypothesis, not a decorative number added after compression.. Open Quantization error metrics in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Offset-binary coding — Offset-binary coding Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101. Prerequisites
Unsigned modular arithmetic — supplies the representation or validity rule used above. Interpretation contract — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Do not assume an INT4 label defines offset versus two’s-complement storage. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Ordering and bias Offset-binary represents signed values by adding a fixed bias before storing an unsigned code: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> With an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>-bit field and the common midpoint bias <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, the smallest signed value maps near code zero and the largest maps near the all-ones code. Unlike two’s complement, the unsigned lexical order of codes then matches the numeric order of represented values. That property is useful in some exponent fields, ADC outputs, sortable binary formats and hardware interfaces. The bias is part of the format contract. Decoding with the wrong bias shifts every value while still producing plausible numbers. The IEEE-754 exponent field is related but reserves all-zero and all-one exponent codes for subnormals/zero and infinities/NaNs, so it is not simply an unrestricted offset-binary integer. Tests should check both endpoints, the code corresponding to numeric zero, monotonic ordering, and rejection or handling of reserved codes when the surrounding format defines them.. Open Offset-binary coding in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Multilevel pointer qualification — Multilevel pointer qualification Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism int** cannot implicitly become const int**: that would permit injection of an actually const object’s address into an original int*. int** can become const int* const*, whose intermediate read-only pointer blocks that assignment. Prerequisites
Const qualification and shallow constness — Access-path qualification constrains nested conversions and member writes.
Used by Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created. Recall and next depth Rebuild the hypothetical pointer injection step by step. Pending: qualification decomposition at further levels. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery. Source and navigation Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map Const applies at each indirection level For a pointer chain, qualification is attached to a particular level rather than to the whole expression. const T* means the pointed-to T is not writable through that path; T* const means the pointer object itself cannot be reseated; const T* const combines both. The distinction becomes safety-critical at multiple levels. Converting T** to const T** is not generally safe: if it were allowed, code could store a pointer-to-const object into the outer pointer and later write through the original T*, violating const protection. Qualification conversions therefore follow stricter rules than the familiar T* -> const T* case. Engine APIs should avoid raw multi-level pointer mutation unless the ownership/indirection contract truly requires it. Spans, references to containers, output wrappers or typed handle arrays often express the real intent more clearly. A reconstruction exercise should explain each const position and demonstrate the classic unsafe hypothetical conversion.. Open Multilevel pointer qualification in Volume 1

After promotions, equal-signedness operands use the higher-ranked type. For signed S and unsigned U: if U rank≥S rank, convert S to U; otherwise use S if it represents all U values; otherwise use S’s unsigned counterpart. Rank and width are related but distinct. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Template matching and distance transforms — Template matching and distance transforms Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Template matching searches an image for a known pattern by comparing a small reference patch at candidate positions. Sum of squared differences penalizes intensity mismatch; normalized correlation compensates for brightness scale and offset. Direct search costs work proportional to image area times template area, while convolution or Fourier methods can accelerate broad searches. Rotation and scale changes require transforming the template or searching additional parameters. For contour-based matching, a distance transform stores each pixel’s distance to the nearest edge. A template edge point then receives a low cost when it lands near an observed contour even if the exact pixels do not align. The chamfer score sums these distances over template points. These methods suit industrial inspection where the target geometry is known, but need explicit thresholds for occlusion, deformation, and false positives. Prerequisites
Convolution and filter footprints Edge localization and subpixel contours
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference
Full teaching explanation Recognition, templates, and industrial matching. Open Template matching and distance transforms in Volume 2
