Numerical reliability figures and their explanations
N10-7 · Summation is an algorithm, not just a plus sign — Exact real sum is 10000. The three-term counterexample shows why Kahan is not an exact-arithmetic guarantee. Strict IEEE-style evaluation is assumed; reassociation can invalidate compensation. N10-8 · More polynomial degree does not guarantee a better picture — Both interpolants match every node. Their behaviour between nodes differs. Chebyshev extrema reduce this example’s endpoint oscillation; this comparison is not a universal interpolation error bound. N10-9 · Bézier and Hermite can tell the same curve story — Use Hermite tangents 3(P1−P0) and 3(P3−P2) for this cubic Bézier curve. The control polygon bounds the curve through nonnegative weights summing to one; inner control points need not lie on the curve. N10-10 · A root solver needs both progress and a safety argument — The error comparison uses cos(x)−x with specified starting values. Bisection has a shrinking bracket; Newton and secant need additional hypotheses. The plotting floor is explicitly shown rather than interpreted as continuing convergence. N10-11 · Arbitrary sample counts need full-domain support — Left: choosing the first five of nine equal cells and averaging equally gives E[y] = 0.3, while the uniform-square value is 0.5. Right: one point per marginal bin is a midpoint illustration; randomized LHS jitters and permutes appropriately, and is not full multidimensional stratification. N10-12 · Algebraically equal formulas can have unequal numerical error — The reference uses 90-digit Decimal arithmetic and compares binary64 formulas for b from 100 to 10¹⁶. This bounded example illustrates cancellation, not a complete robust quadratic solver.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Integrity and authenticity — Integrity and authenticity Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message. Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash. A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> and compute a tag such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mi>K</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash. A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available. HMAC construction For hash block size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> </math>, normalize key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> to one block, then compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mi>K</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>o</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message. tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector. Key management is part of authenticity A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:
the key is embedded publicly in the executable; keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation; a compromised key is never rotated; comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment; replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.
Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols. Production boundary The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code. Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.. Open Integrity and authenticity in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Fixed-width integer types — Fixed-width integer types Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism Native bool is not a portable wire/GPU field; validate an explicit zero/one encoding. Floating type names do not guarantee exact IEEE formats; is_iec559 alone does not identify binary32. int need not be32 bits; sizeof(char)==1 measures a C++ byte and CHAR_BIT is at least8. Plain char is distinct from signed/unsigned char and its signedness is implementation-defined. size_t represents object sizes, not a stable serialized field. Query numeric_limits for digits, lowest, max and floating capabilities. A container’s size_type is not universally required to be exactly size_t. <cstdint> exact-width types express binary layout contracts; least and fast families have different portability goals. When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Exact-width typedefs are optional on implementations lacking suitable types. size_t represents object sizes and ptrdiff_t differences. Prerequisites
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent. Byte and octet — An octet is exactly eight bits.
Used by
Scoped enums and validated domains — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract. Bit casting and representation — uses fixed-width integer types to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy. Integral promotion — uses fixed-width integer types as part of its representation or reasoning. Serialization — uses fixed-width integer types as part of its representation or reasoning. Guest and host integer domains — uses fixed-width integer types as part of its representation or reasoning. Byte swapping and network order — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation. ABI and object layout — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.
Recall and next depth Explain fixed-width integer types without the label, work the example above, then state the assumption whose removal would change the result. Pending: Full lifetime replacement, ownership/concurrency policies and cross-target ABI experiments; the opening examples do not establish those later guarantees. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Page faults and demand paging — Page faults and demand paging Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism A memory fault requires OS intervention when current translation/protection state cannot satisfy access. Valid demand loading, zero-fill, or copy-on-write may install/alter mapping then retry. Invalid addresses or denied permissions may fail instead. A fault need not perform disk I/O; a TLB miss need not fault at all. Prerequisites
Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.
Used by
Copy-on-write — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Basis coordinates and dimension — Basis coordinates and dimension Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7 Definition and mechanism Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>B</mi> </msub> </math>. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example. A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so its slanted-basis coordinates are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two. Prerequisites
Vector spaces subspaces and span — Reachability and closure establish the spanning and independence questions.
Used by
Matrices as linear maps and basis images Norms lengths and induced distances — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Linear systems and fundamental subspaces — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. Spline bases and curve evaluation Additive energy and approximate structure Exceptional projections and dimension ## Recall and next depth
Separate passive coordinate change from active transformation and explain near-dependent basis sensitivity. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Signed magnitude — Signed magnitude Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism The high bit selects sign while remaining bits encode magnitude; this is intuitive but has positive and negative zero and needs sign-aware arithmetic. The high bit holds sign and the remaining bits hold magnitude. Eight-bit +5 is 00000101, −5 is 10000101, and 00000000 and 10000000 both denote zero. Mixed signs require magnitude comparison and subtraction rather than ordinary raw-bit addition. Prerequisites
Positional notation — A base is the number of available digits. Bit significance — LSB means least significant bit, normally position 0 with weight 1.
Used by
One's complement — uses signed magnitude as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Huge pages and TLB reach — Huge pages and TLB reach Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism A larger page covers more bytes per translation. With T same-size cached entries, illustrative reach is T×P bytes. One GiB requires 262144 pages at 4 KiB versus 512 at 2 MiB. Larger pages trade flexibility, availability, fragmentation and fault granularity; the counts alone do not prove performance improvement. Prerequisites
TLB — Larger pages change the amount of memory covered by cached translations. Allocator fragmentation — Coarser allocation granularity introduces space/availability trade-offs.
Used by Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept. Recall and next depth Calculate page counts without asserting a universal speedup. Pending: Mixed page sizes, workloads, benchmarks and OS policy. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reach, fragmentation, and measurement TLB reach is approximately the number of cached translations multiplied by the page size. If a TLB can hold <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math> translations, switching from 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB huge pages can increase the bytes covered by those translations by a factor of 512. That does not make huge pages universally faster. They can increase internal fragmentation, make allocation/compaction harder, change NUMA placement behavior and waste memory when only small portions of each huge page are touched. Transparent Huge Pages may also promote or split mappings asynchronously, so an application should not infer actual page size from its allocation API alone. The right benchmark holds the useful computation fixed while varying working-set size and access stride, then observes TLB/page-walk counters where available. A speedup from huge pages should correlate with translation pressure rather than simply with a different allocator or cache footprint. For engines, huge pages are most plausible for stable, large, densely accessed arenas—not as a default for every allocation.. Open Huge pages and TLB reach in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Fixed-point range and resolution — Fixed-point range and resolution Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism For signed N-bit raw storage and F fraction bits, step is 2^-F and the positive endpoint is (2(N-1)-1)/2F. Required step 0.001 and magnitude 1e6 in 32 bits allow F=10 or 11. Prerequisites
Fixed-point representation — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Coordinate-origin and wider-carrier designs need their own range proofs. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth A fixed-point value stores an integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> together with an implied scale <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math>, so the represented real quantity is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>s</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> For a binary fractional format with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>F</mi> </math> fractional bits, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Increasing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>F</mi> </math> improves resolution but consumes integer range because storage width has not changed. For signed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit two’s-complement storage, the approximate real range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> This makes format choice an error-budget decision rather than a syntax decision. Position data may need large range; normalized coefficients may need fine local resolution. Multiplication temporarily doubles the number of fractional bits, so a production operation needs a widened intermediate or a deliberate rescale, round and saturate policy. Tests should exercise representable endpoints, half-step rounding, overflow, negative values, multiplication rescaling and accumulation. A format can be perfectly deterministic and still be numerically unsuitable if its step size exceeds the physical or visual tolerance of the subsystem using it.. Open Fixed-point range and resolution in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Full adder — Full adder Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Adds <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </math>; sum is three-way XOR and carry is the majority of its inputs. A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in. Sum is their parity; carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. Build it from two half adders: add A,B, then add that sum to carry-in, then OR the two carry outputs. Prerequisites
Half adder — A half adder adds two bits with sum S=A XOR B and carry C=A AND B. Carry and borrow — For N-bit unsigned addition, carry-out means the exact sum exceeds 2ᴺ−1.
Used by
Ripple-carry addition — uses full adder as part of its representation or reasoning. Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags — uses full adder as part of its representation or reasoning. Subtraction through addition — uses full adder as part of its representation or reasoning. Shift-and-add multiplication — uses full adder as part of its representation or reasoning.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Ref-qualified accessors — Ref-qualified accessors Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C009 Definition and mechanism Value-returning temporary accessors provide an owning result through direct construction or member movement. Both const and mutable rvalue policies remain required; the shorter M009 source example does not replace the four-way safe design. Member &/&& qualifiers constrain the caller’s object category. Borrowed getters suit persistent owners; temporary getters can return owning values or be deleted. Handle const rvalues too: a missing const&& policy can expose a borrowed result through const&. Inside && members, *this remains an lvalue. Prerequisites
Const qualification and shallow constness — Access-path qualification constrains nested conversions and member writes. Value categories and materialization — Expression category determines viable binding and whether temporary identity is needed. Temporary lifetime extension — Temporary deadlines constrain returned paths and deferred access.

Reversibility alone does not provide secure encryption. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Carry and borrow — Carry and borrow Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Carry is information leaving the high end of unsigned addition; borrow records an unmet subtraction at a bit position. Architecture subtraction flags may encode borrow or no-borrow. For N-bit unsigned addition, carry-out means the exact sum exceeds 2ᴺ−1. A borrow means a subtraction needs value from a higher position. In an ordinary unsigned subtract, A<B implies borrow. Some architectures expose the complement, no borrow, in their carry flag. Prerequisites
Positional notation — A base is the number of available digits. Boolean algebra — The logical domain is false/true.
Used by
Full adder — uses carry and borrow as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership and non-owning views Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism By-value copies use member semantics, not recursive deep cloning. Rule-Zero composition delegates ownership to members; raw owners must coordinate transfer and release. Copying a pointer/view/handle is not acquiring ownership. Copying span/string_view or capturing a view by value copies only a descriptor. An owning string capture supplies independent storage; a view or handle does not automatically pin a deferred resource. The inline C++ laboratory distinguishes NamedVector::to_array, which copies values into a new array, from ArrayVector::view, which aliases actual array elements without owning them. Neither span nor pointer extends backing lifetime. Ownership and RAII are introduced as next-depth connections, not yet a full exception-safety treatment. M010 makes the distinction operational: an owner is responsible for release; a borrow only accesses. std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr retains a shared lifetime, and std::weak_ptr observes without extending that lifetime. Smart pointers do not remove the borrow/invalidation rules of raw pointers obtained from them. See RAII and resource handles and Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership. An owner controls a resource’s validity and release; a view merely refers to it. Vector owns its element buffer; span does not copy or prolong that buffer’s life. Owner destruction or invalidating reallocation can dangle the span. A reader retaining a span needs stable live backing for every read, not only at construction. Prerequisites
Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid. Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.
Used by
Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Deferred captures and borrowed views Copy semantics and resource identity Rules of Three Five and Zero RAII and resource handles Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership
Recall and next depth Explain why returning a view into a local vector fails. Pending: smart owners, shared immutable data and scheduling/resource pinning. Source and navigation C009 development C008 development and corrections C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map · C007 development. Open Ownership and non-owning views in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Convolution and filter footprints — Convolution and filter footprints Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Convolution combines shifted values with a weighting kernel; its spectrum multiplies transfer functions. Pixel footprints and boundary policies define what is averaged. A separable Gaussian uses two 1D passes; unpadded DFT filtering wraps circularly. Prerequisites
Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples. Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.
Used by
PSF OTF and MTF Multiscale texture filtering Optical flow and time to contact Edge localization and subpixel contours Template matching and distance transforms PDE fields and discrete Laplacians Attention and visual transformers Learned image features and CNNs ## Recall and next depth
Derive the three-tap filter’s gain and constant preservation. Pending: implementation cost, padding and spatially varying kernels. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Textures and surface detail. Open Convolution and filter footprints in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Norms, dual norms and error budgets — Norms, dual norms and error budgets A norm defines a size rule. Its dual norm measures the largest scalar response a linear measurement can produce over the unit ball of that norm. For a covector represented by coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>a</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>∗</mo> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mo>,</mo> </math> and therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>≤</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>a</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>∗</mo> </msub> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> This turns an error budget into a sensitivity bound. The choice of norm matters because different “allowed error shapes” have different worst cases. A Euclidean ball is self-dual: the dual of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>. A componentwise box uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> </math> for the error and has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> as the dual measurement norm. An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> error budget has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> </math> dual sensitivity. Example: if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>0.01</mn> </math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>≤</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>+</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>0.01</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.05</mn> <mo>.</mo> </math> This is more informative than a generic epsilon because it says what perturbations are permitted and what scalar quantity is being protected. Error budgets in graphics and simulation should also carry units. A state vector mixing metres, radians, exposure values and normalized texture coordinates does not acquire a physically meaningful Euclidean norm merely because the values are stored in one array. The metric or scaling must state what “one unit of error” means in each subspace. Full derivation and worked trace: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Bound a measurement using a dual norm. Related: Metric gradients and differential measurements, Forward and backward error, Numerical error budgets.. Open Norms, dual norms and error budgets in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Stable reformulation — Stable reformulation Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism A mathematically equivalent expression can avoid unnecessary numerical loss. sqrt(x+1)−sqrt(x)=1/(sqrt(x+1)+sqrt(x)) for x≥0; at double x=1e16 the direct result is zero while the reciprocal form remains near 5e-9. Prerequisites
Cancellation and loss of significance — Near-equal operand errors motivate exact-subtraction distinctions and reformulation.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive.
Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp Stable quadratic root evaluation ## Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid. Pending: Every reformulation still needs domain, range, conditioning and accuracy checks. Source and navigation M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Algebraic equivalence is not numerical equivalence Two formulas can be identical over real arithmetic and behave very differently in finite precision. Stable reformulation changes the computational path while preserving the intended mathematical quantity. For the quadratic equation, the textbook root expression can subtract nearly equal numbers and lose most significant digits. Computing one root with a sign-aware expression such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mstyle displaystyle="false" scriptlevel="0"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> </mstyle> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>sign</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>a</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msqrt> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> </math> and obtaining the other as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </math> avoids that cancellation in many cases. The same idea appears in log-sum-exp, hypot-style norms, rationalizing expressions, compensated sums, and solving least squares with QR rather than normal equations. A reformulation is not automatically stable: its overflow/underflow regions and exceptional inputs still need analysis. Tests should compare against a higher-precision reference across adversarial inputs, not only ordinary random values. The goal is to show that the reformulated algorithm reduces forward/backward error where the naive expression is fragile.. Open Stable reformulation in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks — Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order. Prerequisites
Derivative as a local linear map Matrix multiplication and composition order Probability density and change of measure
Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Determinants orientation and volume — Determinants orientation and volume Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A square matrix determinant measures oriented volume scale. Zero means rank loss; sign records orientation reversal. Its magnitude depends on scale and is not a standalone measure of numerical conditioning. Reconstruction cue: Uniform tiny scaling can have tiny determinant and condition number one. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area Matrices as linear maps and basis images
Used by
Matrix inversion pivoting and residuals Polar decomposition — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. ## Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example, state its conventions and find an input that violates its preconditions. Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model. Source and navigation Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification University course development Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> </math> in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection. Pose estimation, transforms, and robust fitting · Visibility queries and ray intersections · Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing. Open Determinants orientation and volume in Volume 1

A mask is a selection pattern, not an operation. 0x30 = 00110000₂ names positions 4 and 5. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Binary conversion — Binary conversion Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001 Definition and mechanism Repeated division emits low-to-high binary digits; weighted sums or Horner evaluation decode them. Euclidean division writes n = 2q + r, where q is the integer quotient and r is 0 or 1. Repeated remainders give bits from least to most significant. Zero must be represented explicitly as 0. Horner evaluation reads left to right: accumulator = 2×accumulator + next bit. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Atomic operations and write contention — Atomic operations and write contention Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism Independently meaningful fields sharing a word can require coordinated read-modify-write and can cause unrelated writers to contend. An atomic update is indivisible to other participating accesses under its specified memory ordering. Packed independent flags may share one read-modify-write location: writers can overwrite each other without coordination. Contention means accesses compete for ownership or serialization. Atomic additions can prevent lost writes without fixing addition order. Different valid schedules can produce different rounded sums; deterministic reduction requires a defined tree as well as safe synchronization. Prerequisites
Bit packing — Packing places several constrained values into a carrier. Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Optical flow and time to contact — Optical flow and time to contact Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Optical flow is the apparent 2D motion of image features between frames. Under brightness constancy, a tracked point keeps approximately the same intensity as it moves, yielding the constraint <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mi>u</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> <mi>v</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, where spatial derivatives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> </math> and temporal derivative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> are measured from the image and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is image velocity. One equation cannot determine two unknown components at a single pixel, so algorithms add neighborhood smoothness, feature tracking, or multiple scales. Flow can reveal camera motion, object motion, and looming. For an object approaching at speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>, its image size grows at a rate related to depth; the ratio of size to its time derivative estimates time to contact without separately knowing absolute scale under simplifying assumptions. Texture, occlusion, and illumination changes violate brightness constancy. Prerequisites
Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion Convolution and filter footprints

A cache line is the block moved between cache levels; memory bandwidth is bytes transferred per unit time. With an illustrative 64-byte line, byte-per-bit data stores 64 logical bits, while packed data stores 512. Real line sizes and performance must be measured for the target. Prerequisites

Reordering 24→16-byte records reduces footprint, not necessarily measured traffic or speed. Field reordering and AoS versus SoA separates hot field arrays from full records; TLB caches translations rather than contents. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Atomic publication and durability — Atomic publication and durability Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Publishing a prepared temporary file by replacement concerns observers of the filesystem namespace. Crash durability concerns whether contents and namespace updates survive failures; it needs a specified platform/filesystem protocol. Neither follows from building a vector of bytes. The supplied AtomicFile excerpt is an unverified repository claim, not a tested durability guarantee. Prerequisites
Serialization — Publication persists already-specified bytes, rather than defining their format. Ownership and non-owning views — A mapping or publication pipeline must keep referenced bytes valid.
Used by Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept. Recall and next depth Name the observers and failure model for an atomic guarantee. Pending: Platform replacement semantics, flush ordering, recovery and cross-volume limits. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Executed POSIX durability sequence The durability contract now has an actual syscall-level witness in tools/labs/atomic_publication_durability_lab.cpp. The reference creates a staging file with exclusive creation, writes the complete payload, calls fsync on the file, closes it, renames it within the same directory, opens the containing directory, and calls fsync on that directory before treating publication as complete. It then verifies the final bytes and absence of the staging name. Separate tests reject a pre-existing staging file and a traversal-style final name. This is stronger than “write temp then rename,” because rename atomicity and durable persistence are different properties. The file sync requests persistence of file contents/metadata; the directory sync requests persistence of the directory-entry change. Successful calls on CI are evidence that the operating-system/filesystem accepted that ordering. They are not a laboratory power-cut test and cannot promise identical persistence guarantees on every filesystem, storage controller, Windows API, network filesystem or production asset pipeline.. Open Atomic publication and durability in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Floating-point infinities — Floating-point infinities Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction. Prerequisites
Binary32 — The concrete fields provide the representation used in this mechanism.
Used by
Numerical tolerance policies — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Robust norm and intermediate range — uses this mechanism in its explanation.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the concrete example in the definition and identify its validity assumptions. Pending: Define non-finite input policy before applying a relative tolerance formula. Source and navigation M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth IEEE-754 infinities represent values beyond the finite exponent range and results such as nonzero finite division by signed zero. They participate in arithmetic according to defined extended-real-like rules. Adding a finite value to positive infinity stays positive infinity, while indeterminate forms such as infinity minus infinity produce NaN. Infinity can be useful as a sentinel in algorithms, such as an initial shortest-path distance, because comparisons with finite positive values behave naturally. But it is not automatically a valid physical or engine state. A transform position, mass, texture coordinate or timestamp becoming infinite usually signals overflow or invalid input and should be caught at a subsystem boundary. A robust numeric API distinguishes the floating type can encode infinity from this domain accepts infinity. Tests should exercise overflow, division by zero under the active floating environment, comparisons, finite-value validation and serialization behavior. Fast-math modes may weaken exceptional-value assumptions, so production guarantees must match compile configuration.. Open Floating-point infinities in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Checksums CRCs and hashes — Checksums, CRCs, and hashes Curriculum depth: Reference implemented and known-answer tested · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair A checksum or digest maps an arbitrary byte sequence to a smaller fixed-size value. Different families make different promises. An additive checksum is mainly an accidental-error detector and is weak against structured changes such as reordering or compensating byte modifications. A CRC interprets bits as a polynomial over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and computes a remainder under a declared generator polynomial and parameter set. CRCs are excellent for many transmission/storage error patterns, but they are not cryptographic authenticators. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is designed so that finding collisions or preimages is computationally hard under the security assumptions of the primitive. A hash still does not authenticate a file when an attacker can replace both the file and the untrusted hash value. SHA-256 compression structure SHA-256 pads the message with a one bit, enough zero bits to leave 64 bits at the end of the final 512-bit block, and then the original message length modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>64</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Each 512-bit block expands sixteen 32-bit words into a 64-word schedule and updates an eight-word chaining state through 64 rounds. The important learning boundary is representation: message words are interpreted in the algorithm’s specified byte order. Reinterpreting native host integers without explicit conversion can produce a platform-specific hash implementation. Known-answer evidence tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp implements SHA-256 directly and validates the standard digest of “abc” and the empty message. The same SHA-256 implementation is then used by HMAC, HKDF and a domain-separated Merkle tree. This raises the evidence above “definition present,” but the implementation is educational. It is not reviewed for constant-time behavior, hardware acceleration, fault attacks, side channels or production cryptographic use. What to use for what Use a checksum/CRC when the threat is accidental corruption and the protocol specifies the polynomial/parameters. Use a cryptographic hash when content identity or collision/preimage resistance is required. Use a MAC such as HMAC when a party holding a secret key must authenticate content. Use a digital signature when verification must be possible without sharing the signing secret. Prerequisites Bitwise XOR, Serialization, Endianness. Used by Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Production manifests and transactional publication. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Dependency Map. Open Checksums CRCs and hashes in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Triangle rasterization and coverage tests — Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Rasterization converts triangle geometry into a finite set of image samples. A pixel’s ideal coverage is the area fraction inside the triangle; a center test approximates this integral with one binary answer and therefore creates jagged edges. A directed edge defines an inside half-plane, so three signed edge tests classify a point against a triangle. A consistent tie rule assigns samples exactly on shared edges to one triangle, preventing cracks and double coverage. Supersampling tests several locations per pixel and averages their coverage, trading cost for a better area estimate. Hardware often checks candidate samples in parallel within a bounding box, then rejects or accepts coarse blocks that are wholly outside or inside. Triangle coverage is also the basis for interpolating depth, color, normals, and texture coordinates. Prerequisites
Barycentric coordinates and interpolation Sampling aliasing and reconstruction

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Spline bases and curve evaluation — Spline bases and curve evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Prefix scan and stream compaction — Prefix scan and stream compaction A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math> If each element says how many output records it will emit, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> is the first output slot owned by element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math>. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions. For Boolean compaction, let predicate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Scan <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> to obtain offsets. Every active element with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1]. Parallel structure The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> depth. On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:
scan each workgroup block into local output; record each block total; scan the block totals; add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.
Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct. Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup. Stream compaction as an allocation proof Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues. The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur. Evidence boundary The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing. Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.” Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions. Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, BVH build traversal and workload selection.. Open Prefix scan and stream compaction in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Metric gradients and differential measurements — Metric gradients and differential measurements The differential of a scalar function is a linear measurement of displacement. The gradient is the vector that represents that measurement after an inner product or metric has been chosen. At a point, let coordinate derivative coefficients be collected in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>g</mi> </math>. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>g</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>h</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> If the vector-space inner product is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⟨</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>h</mi> <msub> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⟩</mo> <mi>G</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>u</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>G</mi> <mi>h</mi> </math> for symmetric positive-definite metric matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> </math>, the metric gradient is defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>d</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⟨</mo> <msub> <mi>grad</mi> <mi>G</mi> </msub> <mi>f</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>h</mi> <msub> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⟩</mo> <mi>G</mi> </msub> </math> for every displacement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> </math>. Therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>G</mi> <msub> <mi>grad</mi> <mi>G</mi> </msub> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>g</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>grad</mi> <mi>G</mi> </msub> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>G</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>g</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> In ordinary orthonormal Euclidean coordinates <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>I</mi> </math>, so derivative coefficients and gradient-vector coordinates happen to match. That familiar coincidence hides the conceptual distinction. Example: for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>y</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>G</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">[</mo> <mtable columnspacing="1em" rowspacing="4pt"> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>4</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">]</mo> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> </math> the derivative coefficients are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>g</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>grad</mi> <mi>G</mi> </msub> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> The steepest direction depends on the ruler used to constrain step length. This is not merely abstract geometry: weighted optimization, pose parameters mixing translation and rotation, and preconditioned numerical methods all choose an effective metric. The maximum first-order change over the metric unit ball is the dual norm of the differential: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>G</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mi>g</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>h</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>g</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi>G</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>g</mi> </msqrt> <mo>.</mo> </math> So metric gradients and dual-norm error bounds are two views of the same measurement-versus-vector relationship. Full derivation and worked trace: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#A derivative measures change; a gradient needs a ruler. Related: Norms, dual norms and error budgets, Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks, Hessians and local curvature.. Open Metric gradients and differential measurements in Volume 1

Tail padding follows the final member so array stride preserves complete-object alignment. Under 1/4/1 rules, byte–uint32–byte occupies offsets 0/4/8 with end nine and size 12. This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Undefined behavior — Undefined behavior Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Invalid shifts, out-of-bounds access, signed overflow, division by zero, and INT_MIN / -1 provide no valid C++ execution result; optimizers may assume they never occur. The C++ language imposes no requirements on an execution that invokes undefined behavior. It is not an error value or a guaranteed trap. Signed overflow, division by zero, invalid shift counts, and out-of-bounds accesses are examples. Check preconditions before performing the operation. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: GPU workgroups and synchronization — GPU workgroups and synchronization GPU execution has several scopes that must not be collapsed into the word “thread.” An invocation executes one logical shader instance. Invocations are grouped into workgroups for explicitly shared local memory and workgroup barriers. Hardware may execute smaller subgroup or SIMD groups inside a workgroup. Many workgroups make up a dispatch. A workgroup barrier can coordinate invocations that participate in that workgroup. It cannot create a global barrier across arbitrary workgroups in the same dispatch. If an algorithm requires all blocks to finish phase A before any block begins phase B, use a mechanism that establishes that dependency: usually separate dispatches/commands with API synchronization, or a carefully designed device-wide primitive supported by the target model. Execution barrier versus memory visibility “Everyone reached the same point” and “everyone can now observe the required writes” are related but distinct contracts. APIs and shading languages expose memory scopes and semantics because a control barrier alone is not a universal cache flush. The producer/consumer question is always:
what operation produced the bytes? what later operation consumes them? which execution scopes must be ordered? which memory accesses must become visible? which resource/subresource is covered?
Subgroups Subgroup collectives can exchange values and perform ballots, reductions and scans without workgroup shared memory. They are fast but require care around subgroup width, inactive lanes and portability. An algorithm that silently assumes 32 lanes can break on hardware using a different subgroup size. Shared memory and bank conflicts Workgroup memory is physically optimized for cooperation but has finite capacity and bank structure. Tiling can reduce global bandwidth, yet an unfortunate address pattern can serialize accesses through bank conflicts. Register pressure and shared-memory allocation also constrain occupancy, so increasing tile size is not free. Evidence boundary The canonical notes now distinguish CPU semantic models from native hardware evidence. A CPU prefix-scan or render-graph test can prove dependency logic but cannot prove Vulkan visibility, Metal hazard behavior, subgroup width or driver performance. Hardware claims require validation layers, GPU capture/counters, and device-specific results. Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock. Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Shader buffer ABI.. Open GPU workgroups and synchronization in Volume 1

A sequential n-term sum has absolute error bounded by gamma_(n−1) times sum of input magnitudes. Cancellation can make its relative error much larger. Prerequisites
Unit roundoff — The local normal-rounding bound supplies the error-analysis scale. Absolute and relative error — Discrepancy, magnitude and reference units define sensitivity and threshold significance.
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Virtual and physical contiguity — Virtual and physical contiguity Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Consecutive virtual addresses can map nonadjacent physical frames. Vector’s contiguous elements guarantee adjacent object storage in the process model, not one contiguous physical allocation. File offsets and storage-device placement are separate adjacency notions. Contiguity must always name the space being discussed. Prerequisites
Pages and page offsets — Page identity is translated while within-page position is preserved.
Used by Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept. Recall and next depth Map three adjacent virtual pages to frames 912/17/404. Pending: DMA, physical allocation, IOMMU and scatter/gather. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth A virtually contiguous array occupies one uninterrupted range of virtual addresses. The page table may map those virtual pages to physical frames scattered through RAM. Most user-space code only requires virtual contiguity because ordinary loads and stores are translated by the MMU before reaching memory. Physical contiguity matters at different boundaries: some DMA devices, huge-page mappings, kernels or fixed hardware buffers may impose stronger requirements. Modern IOMMUs can themselves provide device-visible address translation, reducing the need for physically contiguous host memory in some designs. This explains why a large dynamic allocation can succeed even when free physical RAM is fragmented into many regions: the operating system can assemble the virtual range from separate frames and may not commit all of them until faults occur. For performance, virtual contiguity still does not guarantee identical locality. Page placement can span NUMA nodes, and TLB reach depends on page size and access footprint. Therefore contiguous storage is a statement about address iteration and element layout, not a complete claim about physical placement.. Open Virtual and physical contiguity in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Vault Repair and Source Retention - 2026-11-14 — Vault repair and source retention — 14 November 2026 This is the supervised local repair of the active iCloud/Obsidian Master vault, beginning at commit c142869a391c32d55068ddfbf4d4ac11ce52762c. The vault’s existing hidden .obsidian configuration and unrelated Finder/workspace edits are left in place. The three continuous books remain the teaching surface; this record tracks changes and evidence, not a fourth lesson book. Integrated teaching and code comments Computing Foundations now embeds its temporary-lifetime, SE(3) exp/log and paired-inference witnesses at their teaching seams. The misplaced closing fence after the reverse-mode Tape includes is removed, keeping the class inside its C++ block. The statistical witness validates finite inputs, normalizes its sign-flip comparison and checks measurement-unit rescaling; the pose witness exercises its documented near-pi rejection. Graphics now embeds the planar eight-state EKF, 3-D zero-order-hold IMU preintegration and discrete NeRF volume-rendering witnesses. The planar camera is explicitly co-located and aligned with the body. The original 1,842-line perceptual/XR packet is relocated intact after rendering so the mathematical prerequisites precede it. The relocation itself preserves 240,779 characters exactly; earlier wiki-route corrections are recorded separately. Game Engine now embeds the block contact, symbolic subresource-state, rollback, audio and AI witnesses. The new bounded scene-persistence example teaches explicit versioned fields, strict decimal input, stable IDs, forward references, iterative cycle rejection, migration and candidate-then-swap publication. Negative fixtures prove failed loads keep the live scene unchanged. This is an in-memory schema/transaction witness, not filesystem durability or a production scene format. For these added and revised programs, implementation reasoning, state meanings, units, branch choices and limits are explained in comments beside the relevant operations. Conceptual prerequisites remain before code. Existing teaching elsewhere was preserved; this pass does not claim to have re-commented every historical snippet. Navigation, formatting and supervision Retired Mathematics, XR and Systems wiki targets now lead to the actual canonical books, retaining labels and anchors. Four dangling concept links point to existing developed explanations rather than new glossary stubs. The retired rigid-body route resolves to the preserved Foundations section. Independent small-agent reviews exposed the missing camera/body extrinsic assumption, scale-dependent statistical tie tolerance, nonfinite-data handling and an untested near-pi branch; those findings were repaired before final verification. Five existing concept cards also had control-byte/missing-command corruption in TeX. Their GGX/Fresnel, homology, spherical harmonics, impulse/friction and Beer–Lambert formulas were repaired with units and domain assumptions. The source guard compares complete parsed code blocks, including comments, instead of relying on a common first include line or counting only one fence style. The preservation guard pins the actual pre-repair books and permits only the documented route, Tape-fence, closure-statement and intact-XR-relocation changes. It still rejects removal or reordering of other prior teaching. Verification and its limits
python3 tools/check_continuous_code_sync.py checks all 26 declared complete C++/Python programs. python3 tools/check_three_volume_consolidation.py checks the three-book inventory, preserved baseline teaching and historical XR packet. python3 tools/check_vault_links.py checks files, headings, blocks and embedded figures without writing to the vault. python3 tools/check_patch_idempotence.py runs all four retained authoring patches twice in an isolated temporary copy; it fails if a patch still changes an already-integrated book. python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/tests -p test_note_integrity.py tests Markdown parsing, whole-program identity, preservation exceptions and navigation failures.
The eight revised/new C++ labs were compiled and executed with Apple Clang under strict warnings-as-errors, optimized -DNDEBUG, and AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer profiles. The four Python witnesses were executed normally and with -O; their validation survives optimization. Recorded receipts include initial failures and subsequent successful reruns. Final counts and equation/diagram checks are recorded in the private verification checkpoint linked below. The final-pass workflows now have read-only repository permissions and verify the checked-in books. They no longer apply or push repairs. They run on the checked-out revision rather than silently targeting an authoring branch. Native Vulkan/Metal, production-engine integration and human-subject XR evidence are separate; this pass does not re-certify them or every existing code fragment. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure — Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A polygon mesh is a combinatorial surface made of vertices, edges, and faces plus an embedding that assigns each vertex a position. Manifoldness is a local connectivity condition: an interior edge belongs to two faces, and the faces around each interior vertex form one cycle or fan. At a boundary, an edge belongs to one face and the vertex neighborhood forms one open chain; each boundary component closes into a loop. A bow-tie vertex with two disconnected fans is nonmanifold even if every face is an ordinary triangle. These conditions let algorithms define an unambiguous local tangent neighborhood, traversal, and surface orientation. Connectivity validity does not guarantee good geometry: valid topology can still self-intersect, collapse to a point, or contain poor skinny triangles. Keep topological and geometric quality checks separate. Prerequisites
Coordinate frames and change of basis
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Half-edge mesh connectivity Quadric error mesh simplification Bounding volume hierarchies Collision barriers and continuous detection Local rigidity and mesh orientation fields ## Full teaching explanation
Surfaces, patches, topology, and parameterization · Meshes, connectivity, and geometry processing · Surface descriptions and Gaussian images. Open Manifold polygon meshes and boundary structure in Volume 2
